results.title: RBI chief says the next financial crisis may start with a cyberattack
results.author: Alina Maria Stan
results.content:
The next financial crisis may not start in a bank at all, India’s central bank governor has warned. Sanjay Malhotra said it could come from a war, a cyberattack or a tech failure, as Bloomberg reported.
He spoke at the Kautilya Economic Conclave in New Delhi on Saturday.
“It may begin with a geopolitical event, or cyber attack or a technological failure,” he said.
AI in the mix
The Reserve Bank of India governor singled out AI, Business Today reported. He said it has made cyber risks worse.
It also brings new risks from faulty models, reliance on outside suppliers and weaker human oversight, he said.
He also flagged high prices for AI stocks. A slowdown in AI spending or earnings could set off a sharp fall in asset prices, he warned.
Last month, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman made a similar point. AI can help catch fraud faster, she said, but it also enables bigger cyberattacks.
India is not alone in its concern. In August, the Financial Stability Board said AI-driven cyberattacks were now the top risk to the global financial system.
In June, the ECB’s Christine Lagarde warned AI could trigger financial crises.
Strong, for now
Malhotra said India’s banks are healthy and well funded, but warned against complacency.
“Today’s resilience may not necessarily imply tomorrow’s immunity,” he said.
The war in Iran has pushed up commodity prices for India. Still, the economy grew 7.8% in the April to June quarter, Bloomberg reported.
The RBI announces its next rate decision on Wednesday. Most economists expect its first rate rise since early 2023, as inflation picks up.

Reserve Bank of India Governor Sanjay Malhotra warned that the next global financial crisis could be triggered by geopolitical conflicts, cyberattacks, or systemic failures linked to artificial intelligence.

### Key Points
- Governor Sanjay Malhotra identified AI, cyberattacks, and technological failures as primary threats to global financial stability during the Kautilya Economic Conclave.
- The Reserve Bank of India official highlighted risks from faulty AI models, over-reliance on third-party suppliers, and reduced human oversight.
- High valuations in AI-related stocks could lead to a sharp market correction if corporate earnings or spending growth slows down.
- The Financial Stability Board and European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde have similarly identified AI-driven cyber threats as top systemic risks.
- Despite current economic resilience and 7.8% growth, India faces inflationary pressures and rising commodity costs due to ongoing geopolitical tensions.

### Why it Matters
These warnings highlight a shift in focus from traditional banking vulnerabilities toward complex, technology-driven risks that transcend national borders. As financial institutions integrate advanced AI, the potential for rapid, automated market disruptions increases, necessitating more robust regulatory oversight and contingency planning.

results.title: This Harry Potter Edition Phone From Realme Is the Coolest Collab of 2026
results.author: Prakhar Khanna
results.content:
Realme is back with another special edition phone in collaboration with Warner Bros. After a color-changing Game of Thrones edition collectible, the company has launched a Harry Potter-themed phone. The Realme 16 Pro 5G Harry Potter Edition pairs themed exterior styling with the standard model’s core hardware and bundles it with a bunch of goodies.
I’m a Potterhead, and I couldn’t wait for my unit to arrive. As soon as it reached my doorstep, I unboxed it and went hands-on with the device. From the unboxing experience to its software, this is a Hogwarts makeover any Harry Potter fan would love.
Alohomora! Unboxing the Harry Potter phone
The new Realme special edition phone comes in a chest-shaped box that resembles Harry’s Hogwarts trunk. Unfortunately, casting the Alohomora spell doesn’t unlock it; you’ll need to use your thumbs, like any other Muggle. Once unlocked, the neat presentation screams of “You’re a wizard, Harry!” and pulls you into the world of Harry Potter.
More from CNET
On the left side, you’ll find a brown box carrying the phone case and a SIM-ejector tool, both of which carry the Harry Potter branding with the Hogwarts crest. Put your wand on the box (you don’t get one with the phone), incant “Accio,” and… yeah, it does nothing.
You need to pull out the case, which is in a matching brown color. And that’s when you start getting to a number of other fun goodies thrown in for Harry Potter fans.
Moving to the right side, there’s another rectangular cardboard holder with the Sorting Hat logo on top of it. Inside, you get the Hogwarts letter, Platform Nine and Three-Quarters train ticket, bookmarks of each house and four postcards.
The letter carries a wax-like stamp on the back, while the bookmarks come with a holder, where you can place your favorite house’s emblem. I added the Hufflepuff badge to it, and it’s now my favorite bookmark.
Move the rectangular holder out of the way and you’re greeted with the phone itself. But before reaching the device, I must tell you, Realme has also color-coded the charger and wire to match the theme. This is worth a mention because several phone collaborations limit the theme to the device and collectibles, leaving the phone accessories plain white. But that’s not the case here and I appreciate it.
A customized Harry Potter-styled phone
With a simple swish and flick, wizards and witches can use the Wingardium Leviosa spell and the phone levitates out of the box. However, Muggles will need to pick it up like any other device. The phone itself continues the theme with gold accents on the dark brown design. There are plenty of hidden Harry Potter references that are delightful to uncover.
Starting with the camera module, it has two prominent camera rings with a little golden diamond between them. Look closely, and you’ll find they resemble Hedwig’s eyes and nose. The camera module’s gold-colored deco looks great against the brown rear panel, which has a leather-like texture. It feels nice in the hand.
The rear panel also has a diamond pattern, which, according to Realme, is inspired by wizard’s chess from the books and movies. It imprints the four-house crest along with the “Draco Dormiens Nunquam Titillandus” motto and the Harry Potter and Realme logos, which are inscribed underneath.
Put it under the sun and you’ll see the crest light up in the house-specific colors. Realme calls it the Quadra Light-Sensing Color-changing Tech, which lights up specific areas when you shine a UV light over it. Also (I almost missed this), the right side of the phone has “Welcome to Hogwarts” engraved into it.
The references don’t end here. Realme’s Harry Potter-fication runs deeper. When you power on the phone, there’s a Harry Potter boot animation and a custom letter wax fingerprint animation.
Then you’re greeted with a Hogwarts-specific UI, with the castle on the wallpaper and more than 30 custom icons. For example, the Phone app is a red telephone booth, whereas the Notes app is a quill. Even the Google apps’ icons are customized to match the theme.
What about the specifications?
I haven’t used the Realme 16 Pro 5G Harry Potter Edition as my full-time phone yet, but it packs impressive specifications. You get a 6.78-inch AMOLED screen with a 1.5K resolution and a 144Hz refresh rate. It boasts up to 6,000 nits in peak brightness. While I haven’t tested it, the screen was easily legible under direct sunlight.
This special-edition Realme phone is powered by the MediaTek Dimensity 7300-Max chip, paired with 12GB of RAM and 256GB of onboard storage.
You get a 200-megapixel primary camera, accompanied by an 8-megapixel ultrawide-angle sensor with a 112-degree field of view. On the front is a 50-megapixel selfie shooter. To top it off, the phone packs a 7,000-mAh battery with support for 80-watt fast charging. It runs a customized version of Realme UI 7.0 based on Android 16. It is limited to 5,000 units and is priced at INR 62,999 (~$655) in India. Harry Potter fans in the US won’t be able to buy this one, but Google’s Pixel phones recently received Harry Potter theme packs that add their own magical customizations.
It is 2026. It’s only fair for Hogwarts to finally adopt smartphones in addition to using Floo Powder to communicate. The Realme 16 Pro 5G Harry Potter Edition feels quite special as a fan of the books and movies. It is evident that the two companies have put a lot of thought into this collaboration.
Realme effortlessly put me back into the realm of the Wizarding World. From the trunk case and its unboxing experience, down to the customized software, I loved every bit of it. Then came the hidden references and collectible items. I have a strong Harry Potter bias, but this is my favorite limited edition phone of all time. It is Riddikulus-ly cool.
results.summary:
Realme has launched a limited-edition Harry Potter version of its 16 Pro 5G smartphone, featuring extensive thematic design elements, custom software, and exclusive collectibles for franchise fans.

### Key Points
- The device features a leather-like brown rear panel with gold accents, a Hogwarts crest, and light-sensing color-changing technology.
- Hardware includes a 6.78-inch 144Hz AMOLED display, MediaTek Dimensity 7300-Max processor, 12GB of RAM, and a 7,000-mAh battery.
- The phone is equipped with a 200-megapixel primary camera and supports 80-watt fast charging.
- Software customizations include a Harry Potter boot animation, themed icons, and a Hogwarts-inspired user interface.
- The package includes a trunk-shaped box, house-themed bookmarks, postcards, and a Hogwarts acceptance letter.
- Limited to 5,000 units, the device is priced at INR 62,999 and is currently exclusive to the Indian market.

### Why it Matters
This collaboration highlights the growing trend of using niche pop-culture branding to differentiate hardware in a saturated smartphone market. By integrating deep software and accessory customization, Realme aims to drive collector interest and brand loyalty among dedicated fan bases.

results.title: Payments firm OpenPayd targets year-end Nasdaq listing to fund U.S. expansion and acquisitions
results.author: Will Canny
results.content:
Payments firm OpenPayd targets year-end Nasdaq listing to fund U.S. expansion and acquisitions
CEO Iana Dimitrova said OpenPayd aims to launch in the U.S. by April 2027 and is eyeing deals to add licenses and technology.
- OpenPayd expects its merger with Titan Acquisition Corp. to close by year-end, subject to regulatory and shareholder approvals, CEO Iana Dimitrova told CoinDesk.
- The company is preparing to launch its infrastructure for U.S. customers by April 2027, after bringing 43 state money transmitter licenses into its group.
- The payments firm reported $73 million in revenue for its latest financial year, while Dimitrova said a listing would help fund expansion and acquisitions.
OpenPayd expects to complete its planned Nasdaq listing by the end of the year as it prepares to enter the U.S. market and pursue further acquisitions, CEO Iana Dimitrova told CoinDesk in an interview.
The London-based payments infrastructure company is in the final stages of the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission’s review of its proposed merger with Titan Acquisition Corp., Dimitrova said.
She expects the deal to close this year, barring a significant external disruption. The transaction still requires the registration statement to become effective and approval from Titan shareholders, among other conditions. OpenPayd would trade under the ticker OP.
The U.S. has become a more attractive market for crypto companies as it develops rules for digital assets and stablecoins. The GENIUS Act established a federal framework for payment stablecoins, while the SEC has proposed rules tailored to some crypto assets. For companies such as OpenPayd, that shift creates an opening to sell payments infrastructure to businesses connecting traditional finance with blockchain networks, even as broader market-structure legislation remains unresolved.
Crypto firms are taking different paths to the public markets: stablecoin payments company RedotPay is pressing ahead with U.S. IPO preparations, having recently completed a financial audit. Others are waiting, with Kraken parent Payward pushing its listing back to the second quarter of 2027 at the earliest, CoinDesk reported.
OpenPayd has integrated with Circle Payments Network for cross-border payments and joined Fireblocks’ payments network, where other participants can access its fiat infrastructure.
The company is a “global infrastructure platform for modern money movement,” Dimitrova said, and “there is no public market competitor that has the same combination of fiat and stablecoin capabilities that OpenPayd can deliver today.”
The listing would help fund U.S. expansion, with OpenPayd aiming to launch services for customers there by April 2027, she added.
U.S. launch takes shape
The company took a step toward that launch last month by bringing MSB USA Inc. and its 43 state money transmitter licenses under the OpenPayd group.
OpenPayd provides businesses with access to accounts, foreign exchange and domestic and international payments, alongside infrastructure for moving between traditional currencies and stablecoins. It counts crypto exchange Kraken, market maker B2C2 and trading platform OKX among the companies using its payments infrastructure
The firm reported $73 million in revenue for the year ended April 30, 2026, up from $57 million a year earlier, according to an investor presentation. The company reported $13 million in EBITDA and a $2.8 million net loss for the latest year.
The reported net loss of $2.8 million is entirely attributable to $5.8 million of one-time transaction costs relating to the proposed business combination, a company spokesperson said in emailed comments.
Dimitrova said the U.S. offers opportunities in both cross-border payments and stablecoin services.
She described delays to U.S. digital-asset market-structure legislation as a setback, but said they had not changed OpenPayd’s decision to expand there.
More deals on the agenda
Acquisitions may play a larger role as the company enters new markets.
OpenPayd is interested in businesses that would add licenses or technology and allow it to launch faster than building those capabilities from scratch, Dimitrova said.
A listing would give it both access to capital and publicly traded shares to use in deals and partnerships. The company is also considering a private placement ahead of the merger to secure funding for its growth plans, she said.
Under the announced terms of the Titan deal, OpenPayd’s implied pro forma equity value could reach $1.1 billion.
“Few markets can match the energy and ambition of the U.S.,” Dimitrova said. “We want to harness that momentum to take OpenPayd from European success to global scale.”

results.summary:
London-based payments infrastructure firm OpenPayd expects to complete its Nasdaq listing via a merger with Titan Acquisition Corp. by year-end to fund its planned 2027 U.S. market expansion.

### Key Points
- OpenPayd aims to finalize its merger with Titan Acquisition Corp. by the end of the year, pending regulatory and shareholder approvals.
- The company plans to launch U.S. operations by April 2027, supported by 43 state money transmitter licenses recently acquired through MSB USA Inc.
- Financial reports show the firm generated $73 million in revenue for the fiscal year ending April 30, 2026.
- The proposed business combination implies a pro forma equity value of approximately $1.1 billion for the payments provider.
- OpenPayd intends to use capital from the public listing to pursue strategic acquisitions of technology and additional licensing.

### Why it Matters
The move highlights the growing interest among global fintech firms in capturing the U.S. market as domestic digital asset regulations begin to take shape. By securing a public listing, OpenPayd gains the necessary capital and currency to compete with established players in the evolving intersection of traditional finance and blockchain.

results.title: New Colorado neighborhood could offer glimpse into the future of home energy use
results.author: Phil McKenna, Inside Climate News
results.content:
A new residential development south of Denver is the testing ground for an unusual partnership that could transform home heating and cooling across the country.
Dandelion Energy, a geothermal startup, and Lennar, one of the nation’s largest homebuilders, recently completed construction of nearly 100 homes at the base of Colorado’s Front Range, each equipped with its own ground-source heat pump. The systems use less electricity than even the most efficient air-source heat pumps, potentially helping Colorado meet its climate goals while reducing peak energy demand and eliminating the need for new gas pipelines.
Ground-source heat pumps draw on steady temperatures belowground to help heat and cool buildings. However, the projects’ custom designs and drilling requirements—homes typically require one or more boreholes drilled several hundred feet deep—are pricey. Drilling alone often costs more than $10,000.
Dandelion, a company that got its start at X—a “moonshot” research and development subsidiary of Alphabet, Google’s parent company—says it can complete geothermal heating and cooling projects twice as fast and at half the cost of similar installations.
The company is “taking a kind of mass market and maximally efficient lens to what has historically been a bespoke kind of custom, high-end product,” said Dan Yates, Dandelion Energy’s CEO and chairman.
Earlier this year at Lennar’s Ken Caryl Ranch development, Dandelion’s drill team demonstrated a lightweight rig designed to quickly move from lot to lot, drilling boreholes and installing polyethylene pipe across the sprawling housing development before building foundations are poured.
Each home gets a single bore between 200 and 500 feet deep, where temperatures are approximately 50 degrees Fahrenheit year-round. Water circulating through the pipe is warmed or cooled by the surrounding earth before a heat pump installed in the basement of each new home provides additional heating or cooling depending on the time of year.
Dandelion’s drilling team can complete boreholes for one or more homes per day. If they had to drill a similar installation elsewhere for a single building, they could lose an entire day simply transporting the rig to and from the site.
Installing the devices across dozens of similar new homes at once also eliminates the need for custom plans for each building and avoids potentially costly retrofits to the buildings’ heating, ventilation, and air conditioning systems.
The end result is a highly efficient heating and cooling system that Dandelion says outcompetes air-source heat pumps and conventional gas heating systems. This is especially true during cold snaps, when energy demand peaks and ground-source heat pumps use a quarter as much electricity as air-source heat pumps, Yates said.
It’s “the only system that actually reduces peak demand and electrifies homes at the same time,” he said.
The Ken Caryl Ranch development is part of a larger initiative the company launched with Lennar in 2025 to install geothermal heating and cooling at more than 1,500 homes in Colorado over two years. Dandelion hopes to scale up to 10,000 homes per year nationwide in the coming years.
“Our mission at Dandelion is to mainstream geothermal, and we think that the time has finally arrived for that to happen,” Yates said.
Just over a million U.S. homes have ground-source heat pumps, with approximately 100,000 new installations each year, according to a 2025 U.S. Department of Energy report. The agency found that geothermal heating and cooling could reach 7 million homes by 2035. Doing so would reduce winter peak energy demand by more than 40 gigawatts nationwide, resulting in roughly $4 billion in annual savings in U.S. electric grid costs, according to the report.
Ground-source heat pumps currently make up just a small fraction of new home heating and cooling systems. By contrast, 3.6 million air-source heat pumps were sold in the U.S. last year, outpacing gas furnace sales for the fourth year in a row, said Yara van Ingen, an associate with BloombergNEF’s building decarbonization team.
Ground-source heat pumps are economically viable across the continental United States, according to a study published this month in the journal iScience that considered incentives, energy costs and local climate and subsurface conditions.
“It is technically possible everywhere, and there is economic potential across all states,” said Juliet Simpson, a former research engineer at the National Laboratory of the Rockies and the study’s lead author.
A primary challenge for ground-source heat pumps is their upfront cost, which averages around $25,000 for a typical new home, according to the Energy Department report. Van Ingen added that space constraints, especially in dense urban environments, as well as permitting requirements that vary across the U.S. can also complicate borehole drilling.
Dandelion and Lennar, an investor in the geothermal company, are among those working to lower costs. But incentives and policy changes also help. An energy efficiency program by Xcel Energy, Colorado’s largest gas and electric utility company, provides approximately $25,000 per home for new, high-efficiency buildings with a ground-source heat pump to offset added building and heat pump costs.
“For large neighborhoods with hundreds of homes, builders may receive seven-figure rebate amounts,” an Xcel spokesperson said in a written statement.
The rebates help Xcel advance its climate goals and meet Colorado’s Clean Heat Standard requirement to reduce greenhouse gas emissions 22 percent below 2015 levels by 2030.
Colorado also provides a $2,000 tax credit for ground-source heat pumps and requires homebuilders to pay for new gas service expansion pipes, costs that are not incurred if developers build all-electric homes.
Policies that incentivize high-efficiency electric heating and cooling while discouraging fossil fuel use in homes are intended to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from buildings, said Will Toor, executive director at the Colorado Energy Office.
Other states and utility companies also offer incentives for ground-source heat pumps, including Maryland, where Dandelion recently announced plans to install the technology in 129 new homes. In addition, commercial ground-source heat pump projects are now eligible for federal tax credits that cover 30 percent or more of total installation costs.
“The economics just look better and better,” Jessica Silber-Byrne, senior manager of thermal energy networks for the Building Decarbonization Coalition, a nonprofit organization working to eliminate the use of fossil fuels in buildings. “There is a combination of both incentives and market signals that suggest that this is about to really take off.”
results.summary:
Dandelion Energy and homebuilder Lennar are partnering to install ground-source heat pumps in over 1,500 Colorado homes, aiming to make geothermal heating a cost-effective, mass-market residential standard.

### Key Points
- Dandelion Energy and Lennar completed nearly 100 geothermal-equipped homes at Colorado’s Ken Caryl Ranch, with plans for 1,500 total installations by 2027.
- The systems utilize boreholes 200 to 500 feet deep to leverage constant 50-degree Fahrenheit underground temperatures for efficient heating and cooling.
- Dandelion utilizes specialized lightweight drilling rigs to install systems during the construction phase, significantly reducing labor time and costs compared to bespoke retrofits.
- Xcel Energy provides rebates of approximately $25,000 per home to offset installation costs, helping Colorado meet its Clean Heat Standard emissions targets.
- The U.S. Department of Energy estimates that scaling geothermal technology could reach 7 million homes by 2035, potentially saving $4 billion in annual grid costs.

### Why it Matters
This partnership demonstrates a scalable model for transitioning residential heating away from fossil fuels by integrating geothermal technology directly into new housing developments. By lowering installation costs and reducing peak electricity demand, this approach offers a viable path for utilities and builders to meet aggressive climate goals while improving grid stability.

results.title: People say I don't look like a multimillionaire. Good — I'm not trying to.
results.author: Kelly Burch
results.content:
This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Tori Dunlap, founder of Her First $100K and author of "Financial Feminist." It has been edited for length and clarity.
My parents were very good at teaching me about money, not just by what they said, but by what they did. They were middle-class — by no means rich — but they made very smart financial decisions and equipped me with a lot of financial skills.
By college, I was the friend whom other friends came to ask about money. I set myself a very public goal of saving my first $100,000 when I was 25 — which I achieved. By 27, I was a millionaire, and now, at 32, I'm a multimillionaire.
Yet I don't look or act the way many believe a multimillionaire should. Here's what I refuse to spend on — and what's become even more important to me as I build wealth.
I don't spend on signifiers of wealth
I'm often told online that I don't look like a multimillionaire should. My hair, for example. If I'm going to be on television, I'll get it blown out. But when I'm creating content for my community, it's often pulled back.
I get my hair done about every three months, which is more than most people. Yet I'm not going to spend the money — or, more importantly to me these days, the time — to have it done constantly. It's just not a priority for me when I have a company to run.
I drive a 12-year-old Toyota
I still drive the same Toyota RAV4 that I went into debt to purchase when I was 22. It's a cute car, it's dependable, and it does everything I need it to.
Maybe I'll change my mind and get a flashier car in the future. It's fine for people to change their minds about what's important to them. But I'm not going to buy a luxury car just to show my wealth.
I rented until last year
Until last year, I rented an apartment even though I was a multimillionaire. I could afford to buy, but I didn't have the time to search for a house.
Then, my landlord decided to sell. That happened to me twice in a row, and made me realize I was willing to invest the time to find a house I love. As I've built wealth, time has become the currency that matters most to me.
I don't think there are silly purchases — just ones we don't think about
I'll never be the financial expert telling you that spending on lattes is stupid. I'm not saying that spending on hair, cars, or homes is silly either.
What's stupid, to me, is spending on things that don't matter to you. If you're buying a certain bag, vehicle, or home just to keep up with the Joneses and look wealthy, you're not being intentional.
In my book, "Financial Feminist," I say that we don't need to stop spending money. But we do need to stop spending on things that we don't care about.
I indulge, but not always publicly
I spend pretty unabashedly on travel. To me, it's one of the most important things.
I'm also proud of the house I bought last year. It's newly renovated and has a beautiful view. Yet, I don't share it online because my privacy is more important to me than showcasing my home. I've been very intentional about keeping some things private, including my partner and house.
My markers of success aren't material
The vision we've been sold of financial success is sexy: it's designed bags, sleek blowouts, and marble columns. I'm out here showing a different version of success.
For me, success means having enough financial security that I never have to be in a situation that doesn't respect me. I want to be able to donate to causes I believe in, and always pick up the check for friends and family without worrying about it.
Women in my community have been able to leave abusive relationships or toxic workplaces because of their financial independence. They can improve their communities and families. For them — and me — those markers of success matter so, so much more than any material markers of wealth.

results.title: US court halts AI nude-image ban challenged by Musk
results.author: RT
results.content:
US court halts AI nude-image ban challenged by Musk
A US appeals court has blocked Minnesota’s ban on AI-generated fake nude images, handing Elon Musk’s xAI an early victory in its free-speech challenge to the law.
The state’s anti-nudification legislation – the first in the nation – which took effect last month, targets apps and websites that enable non-consensual sexualized deepfakes, with fines of up to $500,000 per image. It was spearheaded by state Senator Erin Maye Quade after a man allegedly used social media photos to create explicit images of more than 80 women without their consent. Quade likened the measure to longstanding laws against peeping through windows to take photographs.
Musk’s xAI challenged the law in July on First Amendment grounds, calling it an “overbroad, content-based ban on free speech” and warning that penalties could run into the billions of dollars.
This comes as the company faces allegations involving the content the law targets. A class-action lawsuit proposed earlier this year claims that xAI’s Grok Imagine was used to create and distribute child sexual abuse material from real images, and accuses xAI of failing to provide the authorities with information on users who allegedly ‘nudified’ them.
A lower court rejected xAI’s bid to stop the Minnesota law last month. On Friday, however, the St. Louis-based 8th US Circuit Court of Appeals granted an injunction, putting the legislation on hold while the legal challenge continues.
Minnesota urged the court to keep the law in place, arguing that it is needed to combat the “staggering amount” of child sexual abuse material generated by AI products such as Grok Imagine. Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison’s office said it is disappointed by the ruling and will continue defending the law.
XAI previously mounted a similar First Amendment challenge to a California law restricting AI-generated election deepfakes. A federal judge struck it down last year, finding the restrictions, as written, amounted to unconstitutional censorship. XAI also argues that Grok Imagine has “rigorous protections” against illegal content and has begun suing users it accuses of bypassing safeguards to create non-consensual sexual images.
XAI’s Grok earlier faced scrutiny outside the US after users flagged instances of the chatbot being used to alter photos of women into sexualized images without their consent, as well as cases involving minors. The reports prompted investigations and warnings in the EU, India, France, and the UK. Indonesia and Malaysia temporarily restricted access to Grok. X subsequently tightened safeguards around its image-generation and editing tools.
Losing control of AI?
The news comes amid broader unease over rapidly advancing AI, from privacy and copyright risks to threats to the livelihoods of human creators, with copyright disputes already sparking dozens of lawsuits.
Recently, attention has shifted to increasingly autonomous models going rogue and acting outside their intended environments. Since ChatGPT creator OpenAI’s agents escaped a test environment and accessed Hugging Face servers over the summer, models from companies such as Google, Anthropic, and Meta have gained unauthorized access to or attempted to breach systems belonging to businesses, governments, and international organizations.
Just this week, AI research company Transluce said AI agents tried to hack a Canadian government website, although Ottawa did not report a breach. Asymmetric Security separately found OpenAI models accessed data from 55 websites, including those of the CDC, SEC, and International Energy Agency, using tactics such as erasing records that made their activity harder to detect.
AI companies have begun reporting rogue behavior by their models with growing frequency. OpenAI said on Wednesday that its models may have bypassed safeguards or negatively affected systems at more than 100 organizations, significantly expanding the known scale of incidents. Though AI companies say the the breaches have so far caused little or no harm, they have raised questions over whether developers can maintain control as models gain greater autonomy. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei recently called for a “balanced rate” of development to give safeguards time to catch up – an appeal backed by Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.
US President Donald Trump has rejected the idea of slowing AI development, dismissing fears of AI going rogue as “a hoax.” Amid mounting concerns, however, he and executives from six leading AI companies signed a voluntary White House accord on Tuesday pledging stronger safeguards, including measures to prevent models from hacking or accessing systems in unintended ways.

The outcome of this case could set a significant precedent for how governments balance individual privacy and safety against the rapid development of autonomous AI models.

results.title: Muse Creates Detailed Profiles of All Your Friends and Family
results.author: Lily Hay Newman, Matt Burgess
results.content:
Welcome to Kernel Panic!, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.
Meta’s new personal assistant, Muse, has become a viral hit, with millions downloading the AI agent, connecting it to bank accounts, messages, or health data, and allowing it to complete tasks for them. But as Muse takes off among consumers, data from inside the app is providing insight into how it organizes and presents information to users.
In recent days, multiple researchers have extracted Muse’s internal files and dumped the agent’s operating instructions, providing a glimpse of how the system was built and behaves. Meta has maintained that it intended for these files to be accessible in the interest of transparency, and they do provide insight into how Muse responds to prompts and questions about, for example, highly politicized or sensitive topics.
Independent AI safety and security researcher Karan Joshi was able to extract an extensive array of Muse instructions and system prompts by using the regular chat interface to essentially ask Muse to copy and share its own software files. Joshi then shared his findings with WIRED.
One of Muse’s instructions appears to be the ability for it to create “a page for every person in the user’s life.” This hourly process involves compiling data on family, partners, friends, colleagues, “collaborators,” and people you “follow,” the instructions say.
The general idea is that Muse can use its “memory” (aka structured text files) to collect information about your relationships and the important people in your life. It can then make suggestions, like giving pointers on how to improve particular relationships or, say, where to take a coffee-loving friend for breakfast. Of course, it’s not unusual for AI chatbots to track social information in general—people have been asking ChatGPT for relationship advice for years now. But it’s interesting to see how Muse is set up given Meta’s history and vast access to social network data.
“What it seemed like to me—from all these prompts, system skills data, and things that they’re feeding into Muse—is that they want to understand your relationships that you have with real people,” says Joshi. “They’re trying to know you like a friend, which is honestly pretty creepy.”
Muse’s documentation says that a page may start “sparse” and then be filled out over time, potentially including sections like Facts, History, The relationship, In common, Open threads, and Strengthening. Meta’s instructions say Muse should only use the “evidence” it has available, and that invented details are worse than an empty page.
“Where they live, what they do, the threads that recur (the apartment move, the shared savings goal),” the instructions say. They add, too, that the model could record the “dates that matter,” such as birthdays or anniversaries. A person’s history could include backstory like “the trip in March, the argument that got resolved, the milestone last week.”
The instructions also focus on recording relationship details such as “how close they are, what it is built on, how they act with each other, and what it seems to need right now.” The Strengthening section suggests ways a relationship could be improved, including, “A reason to call, a date worth remembering, something they said to circle back on, a way to be there for them that matters.”
“We are giving AI systems much more information about us than we are getting information from them,” says Carissa Véliz, an associate professor at Oxford’s Institute for Ethics in AI. “It’s not only what we explicitly tell them, but what they can infer from us—correctly or incorrectly, both concerning for different reasons—and what they can piece together from other sources of data.”
Muse is architected so each individual user has their own dedicated virtual machine, which stores user data and context. This VM is inaccessible to other agents and users can wipe memories or disconnect external services at any time. Meta says that Muse is also designed to seek human confirmation before completing actions like sending an email or making a purchase, and that it has an audit log where users can see all of the agent’s activity and future plans.
“For any agent to be useful and actually help you achieve your goals, it needs to have context about you and those you interact with,” Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts told WIRED in a statement. “Muse gathers that based on public information and from what you’ve chosen to share, which is how it remembers the person who sent you an invoice is in fact the plumber who you previously hired to complete work in your bathroom or which flowers your spouse said they liked best.”
It’s become common for AI assistants to incorporate some sort of memory feature designed to allow greater personalization in responses and activity. Miranda Bogen, the director of the Center for Democracy and Technology’s AI Governance Lab, says Muse appears to have more emphasis on relationships and personal contacts than rivals’ systems. In general, these tools tend to offer some transparency and editing capabilities, and Muse does as well. If anything, though, Bogen notes that agents and assistants encourage people to proactively share more data with them versus focusing on culling data.
“These [AI assistant] tools are actively soliciting users to plug their whole lives in—their emails, calendars, financial institutions, everything in order to be helpful assistance,” Bogen says. “That’s dramatically more information than people might have otherwise given to some of these companies. The breadth of access to information that these tools have will lead to a ballooning of what they know about users.
Spotted something we should include next week? Let us know at [email protected]. And stay safe out there.
results.summary:
Meta’s new AI assistant, Muse, is facing scrutiny after researchers extracted internal files revealing the tool’s capability to compile detailed, persistent dossiers on users' personal relationships and contacts.

### Key Points
- Security researcher Karan Joshi extracted Muse’s internal system instructions by prompting the AI to share its own software files.
- The instructions reveal that Muse creates dedicated "pages" for individuals in a user's life, tracking history, shared milestones, and relationship dynamics.
- Meta designed Muse to store user data in individual virtual machines, allowing users to wipe memories or disconnect external services at any time.
- The AI is programmed to suggest ways to "strengthen" relationships, such as reminders for birthdays, anniversaries, or topics to discuss.
- Meta maintains that the system relies on public information and user-provided data to offer personalized assistance, such as remembering professional or personal contacts.

### Why it Matters
The integration of AI assistants into personal data streams creates significant privacy concerns regarding the depth of information companies can infer about users' social lives. As these tools become more proactive in managing human relationships, the potential for data misuse or over-reliance on automated social management continues to grow.

results.title: The 3-2-1 backup rule everyone repeats is missing a step, and I found out the hard way
results.author: Tashreef Shareef
results.content:
If you've ever looked into how to properly back up your important files, chances are someone pointed you to the 3-2-1 backup rule. Keep three copies of your data, store them on two different media types, and keep one copy offsite. It's simple, easy to remember, and just about every backup guide on the internet recommends it. I followed this rule for years, and I was confident my files were safe. However, when I needed to restore a backup, I discovered that the files I'd been dutifully copying for months were corrupted. The backup existed, sure, but it was useless.
The 3-2-1 rule has a gap that probably doesn't get the kind of attention it should. The rule tells you how many copies to make and where to put them, but it says nothing about checking whether those copies work. A backup is only as good as its restore process, and without regular testing and verification, you're just hoping for the best.
3-2-1 only counts copies
The most popular backup rule focuses on quantity, not quality
The 3-2-1 rule has been around for a long time. Photographer Peter Krogh first popularized it in his 2009 book on digital asset management. He created it to protect his own photo archives, and the logic was that three total copies of your data (the original plus two backups), stored across two different types of media (say, an external hard drive and a cloud service), with at least one copy kept offsite, is enough to protect against fire, flood, or theft.
The logic itself is not bad. If your laptop dies, you have an external drive. If your house floods and takes both the laptop and the drive, you still have an offsite copy in the cloud. Each layer covers a different kind of failure, which is why the rule has survived for over a decade and still gets recommended everywhere.
However, it only counts copies. It assumes that if you have your data in three places on two media types with one offsite, you're covered. What it doesn't address is whether any of those copies can be restored to a working state. You could follow 3-2-1 to the letter and still be in trouble if your backup files are corrupted, incomplete, or stored in a format you can no longer read.
When a backup is not a backup
If you've never tested a restore, you don't have a backup plan
The missing step that can turn 3-2-1 from a good habit into a complete strategy is verification and testing. If you're not regularly checking whether your backups can be restored, you have files sitting on a drive somewhere, but not necessarily a backup plan.
When backup software reports a successful job, all it confirms is that data was copied without an error the software noticed. What it doesn't confirm is that the data can be read back, that it's complete, or that it will turn into a working system when you need it. Files get corrupted during transfers and storage media degrades over time. Incremental backup chains break so that later backups depend on pieces that no longer exist. None of this shows up until you try to restore something.
Backblaze's 2024 Backup Awareness Survey, conducted by The Harris Poll with over 2,000 US adults, found that 84% of computer owners say they've backed up their data, yet fewer than 1 in 5 (15%) feel absolutely certain their most important files are securely backed up. That's a massive confidence gap, and it tells you that most people know they should back up, and many do, but very few have tested whether their backups work.
A simple fix involves picking a random file or folder from your backup and restore it. Open the files, confirm they're intact, and make sure your backup tool can find and retrieve them without errors. And that should close the biggest hole in the 3-2-1 rule.
One copy should stay unreachable
Modern threats mean at least one backup needs to be untouchable
If all your copies are reachable from the same network with the same login credentials, a single ransomware attack can wipe out everything, including the original data and every backup.
So, we now have an updated rule: 3-2-1-1-0. The two new numbers address the threats that the original rule missed. The extra "1" means keeping at least one immutable or air-gapped copy. Immutable means the data can't be changed or deleted for a set period, not even by an admin. Air-gapped, on the other hand, means the backup is physically disconnected from the network, like a drive you unplug after each backup or a tape you store offsite. Either way, the goal is the same: one copy that ransomware or a compromised account can't touch. Tools like FreeFileSync can create an exact mirror of your files on a disconnectable drive, which you can then unplug and store separately.
The "0" stands for zero errors, verified. This is where the testing step gets baked into the rule itself. Instead of treating verification as optional, 3-2-1-1-0 makes it a requirement. You achieve zero errors through regular integrity checks and restore practices. CISA, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, has noted that many organizations only discover their restores fail during an actual incident, which is the worst possible time to learn that lesson. Running a test restore every quarter, or automating checks on your backup files, is a better way to make sure your data is safe.
The 3-2-1 backup rule is still standard, with one update
The version of the rule I follow now is 3-2-1-1-0, and it's not much harder to set up than the original. The difference is that when something goes wrong, I'll know my backups work because I've already tested them, not because I assumed they would.
results.summary:
The traditional 3-2-1 backup rule is increasingly viewed as insufficient, prompting experts to recommend the 3-2-1-1-0 strategy to ensure data integrity and protection against modern ransomware threats.

### Key Points
- The original 3-2-1 rule suggests keeping three data copies on two media types, with one stored offsite, but fails to account for file corruption or restoration failures.
- A 2024 Backblaze survey found that while 84% of US adults back up data, only 15% feel certain their files are securely recoverable.
- The updated 3-2-1-1-0 rule adds an immutable or air-gapped copy to prevent ransomware from deleting backups and mandates zero errors through regular testing.
- Cybersecurity agencies like CISA warn that organizations often discover backup failures only during critical incidents, highlighting the necessity of periodic restore verification.
- Tools such as FreeFileSync can assist in creating disconnected, air-gapped backups to ensure at least one copy remains unreachable by network-based attacks.

### Why it Matters
Relying solely on the quantity of backup copies creates a false sense of security that can lead to permanent data loss during a system failure or cyberattack. Implementing verification and immutable storage transforms a passive backup habit into a reliable recovery strategy, ensuring that data is not only saved but actually usable when needed.

results.title: What does the advent of powerful AI models mean for mathematicians like me?
results.author: Terence Tao
results.content:
[This is a guest post by Jennifer Taback. This blog post was initially written in a different file format and converted using AI. — T.]
Recently I have read a stream of articles questioning the future of mathematics: what constitutes a proof, what we value, how we retain the human enterprise of creating knowledge. Many of these articles are written by mathematicians making significant progress on the conjectures that shape their fields, whose work is now imperiled by the capabilities of frontier AI models. I am not one of those mathematicians. There are many mathematical problems that I have revisited over two decades, but none will grab headlines. Nevertheless, I care deeply about their resolution, as do others in my field. What does the advent of powerful AI models mean for mathematicians like me? I have yet to succeed in prompting a solution to one of my long-term problems, though AI models have helped fix an incorrect lemma and suggested a helpful reorganization of a paper. They have pointed me in directions in which I had not thought to look, and spurred me to learn new mathematics. Combining AI with the skills I have honed over the years is making me a stronger mathematician.
Journals prohibit AI models as co-authors, but these models have proven to be effective partners for me. I teach at Bowdoin College, a selective liberal arts college in Brunswick, Maine. While I have many wonderful collaborators, none are local. At my college, I have no one down the hall with whom to discuss research questions; mathematics departments at small colleges rarely have two colleagues in the same specialty. AI fills this gap for me. I respond to its (not always correct) answers to my questions, and ask for clarification as I would from a human collaborator. AI makes me ask myself more probing questions, challenging me to dig deeper into my accumulated knowledge and connect it to the broad synthesis the model can often provide. And sometimes AI is just wrong or confusing, as a human might be, and I move on.
Mathematics is a human endeavor, and machine-generated output requires substantial human intervention in order to contribute to our knowledge base. Having co-organized two conferences on “Communicating Mathematics,” I know that every idea that advances mathematics, whether human- or AI-inspired, requires clear exposition, a skill most of us could improve. AI is helping me here as well; it is making my mathematical writing better by catching small inconsistencies in papers I believed I had diligently proofread, and helping me sharpen my arguments. Our profession should embrace responsible use of these tools in the service of stronger communication.
AI has arrived in my classroom too, at an institution that demands pedagogical excellence and innovation alongside active research. I expect my classroom to change more in the next two years than it has in the previous twenty, in unknown and unexpected ways. I am angry at AI for forcing evaluation into the classroom under timed conditions. I do not perform my best under those circumstances and neither do my students; we have narrowed assessment to what we can proctor. Without graduate student assistance, thoughtful oral examinations, for example, are impractical at the scale of my teaching. Faculty at small colleges, even well-endowed ones, rarely have the graduate students and teaching assistants that make such solutions feasible.
Conversations addressing pedagogical changes resulting from widespread access to AI models are proliferating, but they are often convened at R1 institutions. These conversations must be broadened to include faculty from the entire spectrum of colleges and universities, especially those with higher teaching loads and more limited support. I am optimistic that by working across institutions we can strengthen undergraduate mathematics education. Students will influence this work as well; some of my undergraduates have been remarkably creative in their use of AI tools to further their understanding. One student in my cryptography class, for example, built an animation of a WWII-era encryption device that let viewers watch the mechanics and the mathematics unfold together. I have no overarching answers yet. But I want my students to trade their fear of being replaced by machines for the excitement of building what comes next.
I write this with the security of a tenured professor. In a small department where mentoring is a personal responsibility, I hear the visceral worries of my junior colleagues who are unsure of their path to tenure and beyond. Their position is genuinely different from mine, and their promotion equally weighs research and teaching. They are building a record under rules that do not yet exist.
Working toward new standards for the discipline is not an abstract matter. We have to decide what counts as proof, and what we value for publication and tenure. I would like us to disclose the tools we use for research without fear of judgment, while taking personal responsibility for ensuring that our work is rigorously verified, understood, and explained before we disseminate it. We should not abandon lines of inquiry for fear that AI will get there first; second proofs of theorems, whether by humans or by AI, often provide valuable insight into a problem. I do not want to surrender my questions, nor would I want my junior colleagues to cede theirs.
If we do things differently, adopt novel technologies, and investigate new frontiers of the discipline, we will still be producing mathematics. I love what I do, and I feel I am doing it better than ever. I will keep learning and seeking understanding while making the best use of the resources available to me. I do not know what mathematics will look like a decade from now. I know it will be created by people who have learned to ask insightful questions, and I know we are the ones who will teach them to do that, both in liberal arts classrooms and at research universities. Mathematicians will continue the hard work of discovery and understanding using stronger, and perhaps stranger, tools, pursuing problems yet to be posed.
results.summary:
Bowdoin College professor Jennifer Taback explores how integrating frontier AI models into mathematical research and teaching can enhance human productivity while necessitating new academic standards for the discipline.

### Key Points
- Jennifer Taback, a professor at Bowdoin College, uses AI to refine mathematical proofs, reorganize research papers, and overcome the isolation of working in a small department.
- The author argues that AI serves as an effective collaborative partner for brainstorming and improving technical writing, despite the current prohibition of AI as a co-author.
- AI integration is forcing significant changes in classroom assessment, moving away from traditional methods toward new pedagogical strategies for undergraduate education.
- The author highlights the disparity between R1 research universities and smaller liberal arts colleges regarding the resources available to adapt to AI-driven teaching requirements.
- Taback calls for the academic community to establish transparent standards for AI use in research, tenure, and publication to support both senior and junior faculty.

### Why it Matters
The integration of AI into mathematics challenges traditional definitions of proof and authorship, requiring institutions to redefine how they evaluate research and teaching. Broadening the conversation beyond elite research universities is essential to ensure that faculty at all institutions can effectively adapt to these technological shifts.

results.content:
Top Democrats battle over California's proposed billionaire tax
Sanders and Khanna take the fight to Newsom's doorstep as early voting opens.
Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Ro Khanna are heading to California to rally Saturday in support of an initiative that would place a one-time, 5% tax on the wealth of billionaires in the state.
Their efforts to barnstorm the state come as early voting begins, and millions of dollars have been spent to kill the initiative.
The measure would affect roughly 200 of California's billionaires, with the money going to cover federal Medi-Cal cuts. Gov. Gavin Newsom has become its most prominent opponent, arguing that the tax could be dodged by billionaires who could leave the state for another.
Prior to arriving in San Francisco, Khanna told ABC News that he and Newsom are "polar opposites" on the issue. Both have openly discussed that they are weighing a presidential bid in 2028.
“He [Newsom] doesn't want to offend some of the billionaires who he wants to finance his campaigns, and that's the question: Are we going to be a party for the working class? Are we going to be beholden to our donors?” Khanna said.
The congressman challenged Newsom to a debate, proposing holding town halls and talking to voters about this issue.
"I'm happy to debate him on this any time in the state," he said.
Asked by reporters earlier this week about Sanders' visit, Newsom said he has "enormous respect" for the senator, but on this specific issue, "we fundamentally disagree."
In a statement to ABC News, a spokesperson for Newsom said, "The Governor supports a national tax on billionaires and is proud to stand with teachers, firefighters, reproductive health clinics, and others in opposing this poorly written state measure that will harm California.”
Newsom has shared a counterproposal: a national billionaire tax focused on loans taken against assets.
Tech investors have pushed back hard on the measure. Vinod Khosla warned that the state's top wealth creators will leave, and Mark Cuban told Khanna he doesn't understand business.
Khanna pointed to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
"Someone more successful than both of them, Jensen, is perfectly fine paying the tax, and he's driving the economy more than either of them are these days," Khanna said.
Asked about whether he was concerned about the proposed tax by Bloomberg Television, Huang said, "I've got to tell you, I have not even thought about it once. We chose to live in Silicon Valley, and whatever taxes they would like to apply, so be it. I'm perfectly fine with it."
But billionaires have also been opening their wallets to fight the measure. Building a Better California, the flagship organization fighting the measure, has raised over $252 million, mostly from billionaires, according to public financial records. Top contributors include Google co-founder Sergey Brin (who has given $102 million), venture capitalist John Doerr (who has given $30 million) and former Google CEO Eric Schmidt (who has given $27 million).
Skeptics of Proposition 40, the official name for the billionaire tax ballot measure, say that the measure could ultimately reduce tax revenue by motivating wealthy Californians to relocate and take their wealth with them. According to an analysis from California’s nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (LAO), the tax could generate revenues in the tens of millions in the short term but cause decreases in income tax revenue in the future.
No On Prop 40, a group funded by Building a Better California, is running several digital ads. Some of the ads say that the billionaire tax would lead to a decline in tax revenue, while others claim that the measure will lead to the state legislature approving wealth taxes on non-billionaires.
No on Prop 40’s website lists dozens of groups that are members of its “coalition” opposed to the tax. Among them is the California Farm Bureau.
Steven Fenaroli, a spokesperson for the group, says he thinks the billionaire tax will end up becoming “just another tax on farmers and ranchers.”
“When my members are looking at Prop 40, they see this slippery slope that we seem to have in California,” Fenaroli told ABC News.
David Lesperance, a tax lawyer who has helped several billionaires relocate from California, said, "My multi-billionaire clients… said, 'We need to get out of here. That's over a trillion dollars that have left."
Yes on 40, the main group backing the measure, has received roughly $32.4 million, the vast majority from Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West (SEIU-UHW) and affiliated organizations.
Suzanne Jimenez, SEIU-UHW chief of staff, said the campaign expected to be heavily outspent.
"It was part of our plan," Jimenez told ABC News. "I think the spending is actually counteracting what they're intending to do, and it's actually helping us in our conversations with voters."
Several labor organizations, including California Professional Firefighters and California Teachers Association, are against the tax. When asked on a press call why labor groups would oppose a tax on billionaires, Sanders pointed to the media pumped out by the billionaire-backed anti-tax campaign.
“In America today, is it possible for a ballot item to win when it is being opposed by a handful of billionaires who are spending over $200 million?” Sanders asked. “That is the question. Do you still have a democracy in this country, or will billionaires rule?”
Khanna said that the fight over taxing the ultra-wealthy is already playing out in races across the country this year, "and you're going to see that fight explode in 2028."
"Will it hurt me in fundraising? Yes. Will there be powerful interests with big tech money and AIPAC money against me? Yes. Will it be enough? We'll see," he said.
results.summary:
Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Ro Khanna are campaigning in California to support a proposed 5% wealth tax on billionaires, facing significant opposition from Governor Gavin Newsom.

### Key Points
- Proposition 40 seeks a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of approximately 200 California billionaires to fund Medi-Cal services.
- The "Building a Better California" coalition has raised over $252 million to defeat the measure, with major contributions from Sergey Brin and Eric Schmidt.
- Governor Gavin Newsom opposes the state-level tax, arguing it could drive wealthy residents out of California and reduce long-term income tax revenue.
- Supporters, including the SEIU-UHW, have raised $32.4 million to promote the initiative as a necessary step toward economic equity.
- California’s nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office warns the tax could provide short-term revenue but potentially decrease future state income tax collections.

### Why it Matters
This high-profile conflict highlights a growing ideological divide within the Democratic Party regarding wealth redistribution and the influence of billionaire donors on political campaigns. The outcome of this ballot measure serves as a bellwether for future national debates on tax policy and the role of corporate wealth in American politics.

Table of Contents
From a cage fight on the White House South Lawn to the Defense Secretary’s call for testosterone testing of the military, a current of masculine energy has been coursing through the nation’s capital this year, including, it would appear, in some high-level personnel maneuvers within the administration.
As we compiled this Most Powerful Women list, we were struck by how much had changed since 2025. Four Cabinet secretaries—all women—as well as the White House press secretary, another woman, are gone from positions they held a year ago. Not one of them so far has been replaced by another woman.
The loss of women in the executive branch is striking, because in every other corner of Washington, an increasing number are at the helm—so many women CEOs and presidents, directors and senior leaders, that it’s a challenge to pare down all the names.
To assemble this list, we reached out to experts in every field, asking which women are making things happen—influencing a piece of the world, pulling levers, building things, bringing people together, effecting change.
Just as their ranks have grown, what we think of as a “powerful” woman has shifted through the years. At one time, it wasn’t unusual for a woman to be considered powerful, or at least important, by virtue of her husband’s position. Think an engaged wife of a senator or philanthropist. That version of power now seems quaint as women are occupying those Senate seats—as well as executive suites, mastheads, and judicial benches—themselves.
Many have also broken out of traditional, institutional ladder-climbing to become their own spheres of influence, creating their own businesses and brands. So our list includes the CEO of a Fortune 500 aerospace company, to be sure, but also a podcaster whose political connections give her access to the White House, as well as lawyers who broke off from Big Law to start a boutique firm.
As always, politics is a major factor—in some cases, the major factor—in any measure of power in Washington. The ever-changing political landscape means this list is constantly churning.
We realize some of the names are lightning rods—highly partisan women in highly partisan times. There are MAGA-aligned women as well as those who fight the Trump agenda every day. We don’t mean to lift up either side or pass judgment on anyone’s accomplishments. We’re simply shining a light on the women wielding power—in some cases, boldly and loudly; in other cases, quietly and with little notice—in the nation’s capital today.

results.title: RTX 5090 Buyer Asked To Sign A Resale Loyalty Pledge: ‘NO EXPORT – NO EXCEPTIONS’
results.author: Zack Kotzer
results.content:
The AI race has bodied the market for high performance computer hardware. As data centers lock in as much gear as possible, it has left the rest of the world paying premiums on tech that was trending towards affordable just a few years ago. How far buyers are willing to be pushed is yet to be fully tested. One enthusiast in California has raised concern over a loyalty pledge they were asked to sign to buy an Nvidia RTX 5090, promising not to flip the hardware and tying the purchase to government ID.
“Picked up a Powerspec Ai90 prebuilt PC with a RTX 5090 in it,” posted Reddit user Krothic. “Apparently the manager required me to fill out this form and scan my driver license. Said it was a new thing starting just about two days ago. Had no problem doing so but thought it was interesting.”
Krothic purchased their RTX at a Micro Center in Tustin, California. According to the post, the store had them sign a declaration in order to make the purchase. The single page form asks that the buyer guarantee the card will be used for personal or business use, and moreover that it won’t be resold or even given away. The pledge puts a hard emphasis on nationality as well, demanding that the card remain in the United States. The form asks to list a home address, government issued ID and the intended use of the hardware.
What the penalties are for breaching the contract is unclear, but having the device tied to one’s ID would make it easy to trace if caught. In the comments, others sound off on similar scrutiny at other stores, the top comment saying they were grilled by a manager to prove their gamer bonafides (with photo evidence). Others believe the document was spurred by resale value for RTX cards internationally and recent policies from Washington banning consumer GPUs from being exported to countries like China.
While Trump’s chosen nomenclature for “Super Intelligence” is still taking shape, it’s clear that his administration is infatuated with the AI space. Against the tide of dissatisfaction, the White House is pushing for data center construction and further development of LLMs. As much as AI has grown in North America, it’s exploded across Asia, with China’s industry among the fastest growing. Whether for information security or more literal warfare, it seems Washington wants to prevent hardware from freeing up to other countries.
It is likely that retailers like Micro Center are reacting to these new pressures, and that other stores may have to exercise their own measures as well. It’s not the first time Trump policy has had strange repercussions in the gaming space, and AI’s warpath in general has drastically inflated prices on PC and console hardware alike.

- The mandatory form requires buyers to provide a home address and a scan of a government-issued ID to track the device.

- The surge in demand for AI-capable hardware has significantly inflated prices and tightened supply for high-performance computer components.

### Why it Matters
These restrictive purchasing requirements highlight the growing tension between consumer hardware availability and federal efforts to control the global flow of AI-capable technology. As geopolitical export controls tighten, retailers are increasingly forced to act as gatekeepers to ensure compliance with national security interests.

results.title: Google Wants AI Content Fact-Checked, Gemini UTM Tags – SEO Pulse via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern
results.author: Matt G. Southern
results.content:
Welcome to the Pulse: This week’s updates include Google’s new guidance for AI-generated content, UTM tags on Gemini links, guidance on analyzing Q2 click-through data, AI Mode monitoring eligibility, and the latest on two AI Overviews lawsuits.
Here’s what matters for you and your work.
Google Adds A Manual Fact-Check Step To Its AI Content Guidance
Google’s guidance on AI-generated content now tells sites to fact-check it by hand before publishing, metadata included.
Key facts:
On Oct. 1, Google updated its guidance on using generative AI content by adding three sentences to the “Focus on accuracy, quality, and relevance” section. These updates clarify that generative models predict likely word sequences rather than retrieve facts, and call it “critical to manually fact-check and review all AI-generated content for accuracy and trustworthiness before publishing.” The metadata line was also revised to show that this review process applies to titles, meta descriptions, structured data, and image alt text. According to Google’s documentation changelog, these changes aim to bring the page in line with the presentations at developer events.
Why This Matters
Google’s recent update now puts AI-generated metadata under the same manual checks as article drafts. A review process focused only on the main content might overlook other important fields that Google mentions can show up in Search results.
Read our full coverage: Google Tells Sites To Fact-Check AI Content Before Publishing
Gemini Links Show UTM Tags, And Google’s Mueller Sees Them Too
A Reddit user found UTM parameters on links from Google’s Gemini to websites, and Google’s John Mueller replied that he sees them too.
Key facts:
Mueller asked whether Gemini passes a referrer that sites can already track, then offered to forward details about the referrer’s handling to the team, preferably with examples he can reproduce. Roger Montti reports that Google has not documented the tagging process, so it’s unclear when Gemini adds the parameters.
Why This Matters
Tagged links offer a way for analytics to identify Gemini visits without depending on the referrer. By comparing sessions with UTM tags to your referrer-based Gemini data, you can understand how many visits each method tracks.
Read our full coverage: Google Gemini Adds UTM Parameters For Referral Attribution
Advanced Web Ranking Data Shows Desktop CTR Down, Mobile Up In Q2
A Q2 2026 CTR report from Advanced Web Ranking (AWR) shows desktop clickthrough rates down at the top organic positions and mobile rates up, the reverse of its Q1 findings.
Key facts:
Across all searches, the desktop CTR at positions one and two decreased by a combined 5.27 percentage points from Q1 to Q2, while mobile CTR at these positions rose by a combined 6.59 points. These figures add together changes at two positions and are not tied to any specific site. AWR’s tables, based on its CTR tool, which AWR says sources data from Search Console, are used for this analysis. The comparison period spans the end of a Search Console logging error that led to misreported impressions from May 13, 2025, to April 27, 2026. However, the report does not mention this error.
Why This Matters
Any comparison between Q1 and Q2 in your Search Console data also includes April 27, the date when Google reports the impressions error was fixed. Since CTR is calculated by dividing clicks by impressions, keep in mind that this date could be a point where measurement might have shifted before reading a CTR change as people clicking differently.
Read our full coverage: Google Desktop CTR Fell In Q2 While Mobile Rose, Data Shows
AI Mode Information Monitoring Is Rolling Out To All Users
Robby Stein from Google announced that AI Mode’s information monitoring is now rolling out globally for all users. All his examples focused on local topics and shopping.
Key facts:
Stein announced the rollout on X on Sept. 28, noting that Google AI Ultra and Pro subscribers had already been using the feature. Users tell AI Mode what to monitor, and Search continuously scans for updates. It also suggests monitoring tasks during searches. The post describes “info monitoring capabilities” rather than information agents, a feature introduced for Ultra subscribers in June.
Why This Matters
Stein’s June post said updates would include links to the web, but neither it nor the Sept. 28 post explains how Search picks the sources behind an update. Once the rollout reaches your account, setting up a task for your type of business shows what an update looks like and whether it carries links.
Read our full coverage: Google Rolls Out AI Mode Info Monitoring To All Users Globally
Judge Dismisses Penske And Chegg Antitrust Complaints Over AI Overviews
U.S. District Judge Amit Mehta granted Google’s motions to dismiss the antitrust lawsuits filed by Penske Media and Chegg concerning AI Overviews.
Key facts:
In his Sept. 30 ruling impacting both cases, Mehta determined that the plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege an agreement in which Google exchanged search traffic for their content. He also stated that they lacked the legal standing to challenge Google’s alleged maintenance of its search monopoly. Additionally, he found that Penske did not establish that Search and AI Overviews are separate products. The judge chose not to consider the state unjust-enrichment claims, and said the court does not treat alleged harms lightly.
Why This Matters
Mehta wrote that antitrust law isn’t a substitute for lawmakers dealing with the economic upheaval new technology causes. The ruling does not order Google to change how it uses publisher content in Search or AI Overviews.
Read our full coverage: Judge Acknowledges Publisher Harm But Dismisses Google Antitrust Claims
Theme Of The Week: What’s Written Down
This week, the focus is on what has and hasn’t been documented. Google added a fact-checking step to its guidelines, with this change recorded in its changelog. Gemini’s UTM tags appeared in a Reddit thread, while a broader monitoring rollout was announced by an executive on X. The AWR report omits the Search Console error linked to its comparison, and Mehta explained what antitrust law requires a complaint to allege. Any change that’s documented can be integrated into a process directly. For undocumented changes, evidence may include a Gemini-tagged session or a monitoring task you have set up.
