results.title: If my Docker server died tonight, these are the 4 containers I'd rebuild before anything else
results.author: Ayush Pande
results.content:
As someone who loves experimenting with home servers, I’m no stranger to botched projects bringing down my virtualization nodes. However, a lot of my home labbing, data archival, and productivity needs are met by self-hosted services deployed as Docker containers, and losing them would be a huge problem for my everyday tasks. If you’re wondering, here’s a list of applications that I’d deploy first and foremost if my home server ascends to tech heaven.
Pi-hole
After all, it serves as the DNS server for all my systems
When I first deployed Pi-hole on my local server, I did so for its ad-blocking capabilities. And once I got the taste of its DNS sinkhole provisions, I made sure all my devices route their DNS requests through it. But it wasn’t until I began managing a home lab that I realized all the other cool features Pi-hole hides under the hood.
For one, it logs the DNS requests made by my local devices, making it great for keeping tabs on smart devices that may attempt to contact sketchy servers. On the security front, Pi-hole’s blocklists are also pretty effective at restricting access to malware-riddled websites. But the real star of the show is its ability to create local DNS records, which I use in tandem with Nginx Proxy Manager (and I’ll get to this in a bit) to assign custom domain names to my FOSS app stack.
But if my Pi-hole instance breaks down, I’d be in a world of hurt. Even if we leave aside the fact that I also wouldn’t be able to use my local domain names, most of my devices would lose access to the Internet if my central Pi-hole container is no longer operational, which is why I’d attempt to recover it before any other self-hosted service.
Nginx Proxy Manager
The other essential part of my network stack
Call me a noob if you must, but I prefer the neat web-based interface of Nginx Proxy Manager for my local proxy hosts over its CLI counterpart. Since my broke self still hasn’t bought a dedicated domain yet, Pi-hole serves as the local DNS resolver and translates custom domain names to my Nginx Proxy Manager’s IP address.
NPM, in turn, is responsible for forwarding the traffic to the IP address and port number of the right FOSS service. Since I haven’t memorized the port numbers of the services running on my Docker server (nor do I plan to, either), I’d rather bring NPM back online before I redeploy any other application.
Dockhand
I need this neat web UI for my Docker experiments
Portainer used to be my primary interface for controlling Docker environments, but over time, I started to grow tired of its convoluted UI and paywalled features. After cycling through different alternatives, I ended up moving to Dockhand, which packs nearly every tool I used on Portainer in a neat web interface. However, it also has several unique features that make it one of the most important containers in my arsenal.
Besides the usual network, image, and container management options, Dockhand is also compatible with Compose and environment files and can deploy services across multiple nodes. Its notification channels are great for dishing out quick alerts when things go south with my container stack, and this powerful Docker control hub can even automate the container update process.
Couple all that with the fact that I’d be using Dockhand to redeploy most of my FOSS tools, and you can see why I’d want to restore ASAP if my home server goes down.
Nextcloud
With all its apps, of course
Truth be told, I wasn’t too keen on Nextcloud when I first encountered it. After all, it seemed like a self-hosted file-sharing platform, which I didn’t care about much when I could rely on PairDrop for small files and NAS-powered network shares when I had to transfer more than 10GB of files. So, it wasn’t until I saw the sheer number of FOSS application templates and integrations in its App Store that I realized the real utility of this platform.
These days, I rely on the Nextcloud Office + Collabora Office combo to work on spreadsheets, presentation slides, and text documents (including this very article), and that alone makes it an essential Docker container for my everyday tasks. But I’ve also started using its Calendar, Tasks, and Deck, especially since I only recently realized that I could use my CalDAV events to control my Home Assistant devices.
But these aren’t the only tools I’d redeploy when things go wrong
Aside from the Docker containers I’ve mentioned so far, I’d also be scurrying around trying to bring up other virtual machines and services. Technically, I’ve configured Home Assistant as a VM instead of a Docker environment, but I consider it just as essential as my network stack. Then, I’d move on to restoring my data archival services, which include Jellyfin, Immich, Paperless-ngx, and RomM.
As for their media, I’ve stored everything on my NAS and configured SMB shares to let each app access my archives. If you’re wondering, then yes, I’ve also got provisions for my NAS if it kicks the bucket. You see, I’ve configured a 3-2-1 backup pipeline that stores my essential media files and container snapshots on a second NAS that’s thousands of miles away from my tinkering cave. That way, I’ll always be able to restore my self-hosted arsenal, even if an experiment (or just bad luck) breaks every node in my home lab.
results.summary:
Home server enthusiasts can maintain a resilient digital infrastructure by prioritizing the recovery of essential Docker-based services like Pi-hole, Nginx Proxy Manager, Dockhand, and Nextcloud after system failures.

### Key Points
- Pi-hole serves as a critical DNS sinkhole for ad-blocking, security, and managing local domain names for internal services.
- Nginx Proxy Manager provides a web-based interface to route network traffic to specific Docker containers without requiring manual port memorization.
- Dockhand acts as a comprehensive management hub for Docker environments, supporting Compose files, automated updates, and multi-node deployments.
- Nextcloud functions as a versatile productivity suite, integrating document editing, calendar management, and task tracking through its extensive app ecosystem.
- A robust 3-2-1 backup strategy, utilizing off-site NAS storage, ensures that container snapshots and media files remain recoverable after catastrophic hardware or software failures.

### Why it Matters
Establishing a prioritized recovery plan for self-hosted services minimizes downtime for critical network, productivity, and data management tools. This structured approach helps home lab users maintain operational continuity and protect their digital assets against unexpected system crashes.

results.title: Fake Zoom installer hides macOS backdoor CloudSyncD
results.author: Pierluigi Paganini
results.content:
Jamf Threat Labs found CloudSyncD while doing routine scanning on VirusTotal, buried inside a disguised Zoom client. They first spotted it on September 15, clearly still under construction, and within two days watched it move from a private test address to live command-and-control infrastructure on real domains. That’s a fast turnaround for something that started as an obviously unfinished build.
The delivery method is a classic macOS trick, made to look like a normal installer. The disk image opens as a volume called Zoom, with an app icon and an Applications shortcut. The background image then guides the victim step by step on how to bypass Gatekeeper, because the app is only ad-hoc signed and macOS would normally block it.
After the app starts, a fake dialog asks for the user’s password, claiming it is needed to continue the installation. The prompt keeps appearing until the password is correct.
“Once a password is entered, the dropper validates it against the local account using dscl and does not continue until the check succeeds.” reads the analysis published by Jamf Threat Labs. “After the password has been validated a fake progress window reading Downloading Zoom... appears.”
The captured password doesn’t get sent anywhere immediately. It gets base64 encoded, padded with a random amount of filler text, and buried inside a field that looks like an innocent cache value in a fake settings file named data.json. Nothing about that file screams malicious on a casual read, since it’s formatted to look exactly like ordinary application preferences with a theme and a language setting.
The trick used to find the hidden password is also where the file gets its name. After the visible version number, 1.0.0, there are 48 invisible Unicode characters. They are zero-width spaces and zero-width non-joiners, so they cannot be seen in normal text. When decoded, they tell the malware where the real password starts and how long it is inside the padded text. The amount of filler changes each time, so the password is hidden in a different position on every run, while the technique stays the same.
The malware does not download the payload separately. The full payload is already inside the dropper as a universal Mach-O file. It first tries to run the payload directly from memory through an anonymous file descriptor, avoiding writing it to disk. On most Macs, however, System Integrity Protection blocks this method. Jamf also saw the attempt fail during testing and recorded the exact error. When the fileless method fails, the malware writes the payload to a temporary file and runs it with sudo, using the password it just stole to get the privileges it needs.
“The dropper does not download its payload. It carries a complete universal Mach-O inside itself, roughly 756 KB in the development build, and extracts it at runtime. The same payload is also present on disk inside the application bundle, so the dropper has two sources for it. The dropper first writes the payload to an anonymous file descriptor and attempts to execute it through /dev/fd, presumably to avoid writing the Mach-O to disk.” continues the analysis. “In our testing this failed, with the dropper logging /dev/fd spawn failed rc=13. This technique will fail on the majority of macOS systems due to System Integrity Protection. Upon failure, it uses mkstemp to write the file temporarily to disk, then executes it using sudo along with the collected user’s password.”
A cleanup script follows, assembled at runtime from scattered obfuscated fragments and designed to swap in a replacement app bundle before deleting itself either way. In the builds Jamf actually recovered, though, the replacement bundle simply doesn’t exist, so this entire swap mechanism never fires. It’s a feature built and wired up for a payload that hadn’t shipped yet.
The second stage, which Jamf calls cloudsyncd after its disguised daemon name, is a fairly restrained implant once it’s actually running. It doesn’t set up persistence, doesn’t install a LaunchAgent, doesn’t rename itself to blend in the way its own configuration suggests it’s designed to. It just builds a working directory, logs its activity with encrypted records, and checks in with its server every 8 to 16 seconds carrying nothing but a hardware identifier.
The more interesting part is what happens after the malware checks in with its server. The server can send back either a compressed archive to unpack or a complete executable to run. So the backdoor is not limited to sending individual shell commands. It can deliver and run entire programs, which gives defenders a different clue to look for: a suspicious new file being created or executed rather than a series of strange terminal commands.
By the time Jamf published its research, the malware had moved beyond testing and was communicating with two live domains. Both were registered through the same registrar in 2011 and were protected by Cloudflare. At the time, neither domain was detected as malicious. All the samples also used the same encryption key and initialization vector. That means a single sample recovered by Jamf could potentially be used to decrypt the network traffic of other versions of the malware.
“CloudSyncD is a good reminder that although infostealers may dominate the threat landscape, attackers still have use for quieter malware that lies low until further access is needed.” concludes the report. “Its behaviors illustrate how macOS malware continues to move toward native implementations, string protection, and execution paths that attempt to avoid writing payloads to disk, while still depending on the oldest technique available: asking the user for their password.”
Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon
(SecurityAffairs – hacking, malware)
results.summary:
Jamf Threat Labs discovered a new macOS malware called CloudSyncD, which disguises itself as a Zoom installer to steal user passwords and establish a persistent backdoor for attackers.

### Key Points
- The malware uses a fake Zoom installer that prompts users to bypass macOS Gatekeeper security settings.
- It captures user passwords, obfuscating them within a JSON file using hidden Unicode characters to evade detection.
- CloudSyncD attempts to execute payloads directly from memory to avoid disk writes, falling back to temporary files if blocked by System Integrity Protection.
- Once active, the implant communicates with command-and-control servers every 8 to 16 seconds to receive and execute arbitrary programs.
- Researchers identified the malware in mid-September, noting it was actively communicating with two live domains protected by Cloudflare.

### Why it Matters
This discovery highlights the evolving sophistication of macOS threats that leverage social engineering to bypass native security protections. By combining credential theft with a modular backdoor, attackers can maintain long-term access to compromised systems while remaining difficult for standard security tools to detect.

results.title: Gen Alpha won’t write emails when they join the workforce in 2030—research reveals they’ll sent voice notes to their boss instead
results.author: Orianna Rosa Royle
results.content:
Spending hours typing away at emails, making sure the tone treads the right balance of not too blunt or too casual (or that you’ve not sent a single typo to a boss), could soon be a thing of the past. The London School of Economics has warned that the days of the keyboard are numbered.
The science specialist university, together with audiovisual tech company Jabra, studied how voice technology will impact the future of work, and the scientists predicted that by 2028, voice AI will become the default way of working.
In the next few years, the study says workers will be talking to their phones or laptops, instead of typing, thanks to the explosion of AI.
“By the time Gen Alpha enters the workforce, AI will be fully embedded, and their work will be spoken long before it’s ever typed,” Paul Sephton, global head of brand communications at Jabra, told Fortune.
In the not-so-distant future, he predicts typing will be used only as an afterthought.
“They’ll talk to write, then type to refine,” he explained. “And they’ll direct work, not just draft it. Typing becomes editing, not thinking. The first draft of the future is spoken.”
“This isn’t the distant future,” the 2025 report cautioned. “This is the next generation of how we will interact with Generative AI. It’s powered by voice, and it’s coming sooner than we think.”
It’s not just Gen Alpha who are set to win from the shift to voice tech too
Born from 2010 onwards, the oldest of the Gen Alpha cohort is set to join the workforce by 2030. So in theory, they may never know what life at the office was like before voice technology came along. But, of course, they’re not the only generation that’ll benefit from dictating work instead of typing it.
Sephton explained the shift is coming because “speaking replaces typing because it matches how we think: fast, iterative, conversational.” Essential, convenience and efficiency always win. For workers, both current and future, it’ll mean being able to work more creatively.
“Our best ideas often don’t happen when we’re sitting at our desk,” Sephton said, adding that being able to have an AI teammate instead of needing to stop to jot ideas down will help capture every lightbulb moment better.
It’s also a huge enabler for inclusion, he said. For parents on the go, for example, it’s perhaps easier to juggle talking on the phone for work when your hands are needed, than having to type.
Voice tech in the workplace: A threat to productivity, inclusion, and accountability
Of course, an audio and video conferencing company may be optimistic the future of work involves their tech. So Fortune also tapped academics to weigh in.
Fabrice Cavarretta, associate professor of management at ESSEC Business School isn’t totally convinced.
“Voice notes will not fully replace email for several reasons,” he said, adding reading text is faster than listening to audio and more efficient when searching for keywords. “Scanning an email beats playing a voice message.”
But while he thinks those on the receiving end of emails and messages will continue to favor reading text over listening to their peers’ thoughts, Cavarretta agrees voice technology could supersede typing for those sending the messages.
“My anticipation is that voice will increasingly serve as an input method but be systematically transcribed into text within organizations using AI tools,” Cavarretta added. So we will use voice tech to have AI write the emails, but they’ll be converted to text and read as a traditional email—sort of rendering keyboards useless as predicted by LSE and Jabra.
And that’s a key differentiator. Bertrand Audrin, assistant professor in human resource management and organizational behavior at EHL Hospitality Business School warned that unless voice notes are specifically transcribed to text, they can accidentally make the sender absolved of “responsibility and accountability.” When someone sends lots of voice notes on Slack or Teams, for example, it can be hard to trace back exactly what was said and when.
“With voice notes, you lose a part of the ‘set in stone’ dimension you get with written text,” Audrin explained. “If you need to reference an old decision months later, it’s a lot harder to browse through audio than to search through emails or documents.”
Plus, the very nature of recording your live stream of thoughts means a lot of editing later down the line.
If you’re sending as a casual voice note, it may mean re-recording to get the tone and message just right. Even if it’s being transcribed, it’ll still need someone to cut out the “umms” and any tangents. For non-native speakers or those with speaking impediments, Audrin said it’s an even bigger hassle.
And ironically, what’s supposed to make work easier might just make it harder. “The sheer fact that voice notes are easy to record and share can represent a threat to productivity, as this can lead to a communication overload.”
A version of this story originally published on Fortune.com on November 7, 2025.
Read more about the future of work from Fortune’s Orianna Rosa Royle:
- Elon Musk and Bill Gates are wrong about AI replacing all jobs. ‘That’s not what we’re seeing,’ LinkedIn exec says—the opposite is happening
- AI won’t steal your job—but it might cut your paycheck, Europe’s central bank says
- Elon Musk shares 4 bold predictions for the future of work: Robot surgeons in 3 years, immortality, and no need for retirement savings
- Forget the four-day workweek: Despite what Bill Gates and Elon Musk predict, the CEO of the world’s largest workspace provider says it’s not happening
- Gen Zers could swipe millennials’ jobs if they have AI skills, LinkedIn and Microsoft data shows
results.summary:
A new report from the London School of Economics and Jabra predicts that voice-based AI will become the primary method for workplace communication by the year 2028.

### Key Points
- Researchers suggest that workers will increasingly use voice commands to draft content, relegating traditional typing to a secondary role for editing and refinement.
- The shift is expected to prioritize conversational speed and efficiency, potentially allowing employees to capture ideas more effectively while away from their desks.
- Experts note that voice-to-text AI tools will likely transcribe spoken inputs into written documents to maintain the searchability and accountability of traditional emails.
- Academics warn that relying on raw audio messages could hinder productivity, complicate record-keeping, and create communication overload within professional organizations.
- The transition is viewed as a significant accessibility improvement for workers who need to manage tasks while multitasking or on the move.

### Why it Matters
This shift signals a fundamental change in how employees interact with digital tools, moving from manual input to AI-assisted verbal direction. While it promises increased creative efficiency, businesses must balance these gains against the potential loss of searchable, written documentation and the risks of workplace communication fatigue.

results.title: Community banks sue OCC over trust bank charters of crypto firms
results.author: Cointelegraph by Michael Millard
results.content:
Community banks sue OCC over trust bank charters of crypto firms
Community banking group’s lawsuit claims OCC has overstepped its mandate from Congress.
A community banks group sued a US bank regulator, claiming its decision to allow cryptocurrency companies to obtain limited national trust bank charters exceeds the authority Congress granted the agency.
The Independent Community Bankers of America (ICBA) filed the suit Friday in the US District Court for the District of Columbia.
The group claimed the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has granted cryptocurrency firms the credibility of a US bank charter without sufficient safeguards or compliance with normal bank requirements.
“The OCC’s decision to allow companies to obtain national trust bank charters to conduct substantial non-fiduciary activities exceeds the authority Congress granted the agency,” ICBA president and CEO Rebeca Romero Rainey said in a statement. “Congress did not create the national trust charter as a side door into the banking system for crypto firms seeking the credibility of a federal bank charter without the Community Reinvestment Act obligations, consolidated supervision, capital and liquidity standards, and FDIC insurance that apply to insured depository institutions.”
The ICBA is asking the court to return the OCC to its statutory limits, Rainey added.
The OCC was asked for comment on the lawsuit but had not replied by the time of publication.
Cointelegraph reported in August that under President Donald Trump and OCC head Jonathan Gould, the agency has approved or conditionally approved a slew of applications from crypto companies seeking trust charters to expand their services in the US.
Still, the trust bank charters do not allow companies to accept deposits or make loans, distinguishing them from conventional commercial banks, Cointelegraph reported.
results.summary:
The Independent Community Bankers of America has filed a lawsuit against the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, challenging its authority to grant national trust charters to cryptocurrency firms.

### Key Points
- The Independent Community Bankers of America (ICBA) filed the lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia.
- The suit alleges the OCC exceeded its congressional mandate by allowing crypto companies to bypass standard banking requirements like FDIC insurance and capital standards.
- Plaintiffs argue that these trust charters provide crypto firms with federal credibility without requiring compliance with the Community Reinvestment Act.
- The OCC, under former leadership, has conditionally approved numerous applications from digital asset companies seeking to expand their U.S. service offerings.
- National trust charters currently prohibit firms from accepting traditional deposits or issuing commercial loans.

### Why it Matters
This legal challenge highlights a growing tension between traditional financial institutions and the expanding regulatory footprint of digital asset companies. The court's ruling could force federal regulators to tighten oversight of crypto firms or potentially revoke the pathways currently used by these companies to gain federal banking status.

results.title: 6 Popular Used Chevrolet Hybrids Ranked By MPG
results.author: staff@jalopnik.com (Charles Krome)
results.content:
6 Popular Used Chevrolet Hybrids Ranked By MPG
If we only focused on new Chevy hybrids, this would be a very short article. The Bowtie brand currently sells only one hybrid vehicle in the United States: the Corvette. However, it is available in two different variants — both blending V8 muscle with electrified hybrid torque. The more fuel-efficient of the two trims is the 2027 Chevrolet Corvette Grand Sport X that the EPA lists at 15 mpg city/24 mpg highway/18 mpg combined, while the brand's hybrid range-topper is the Corvette ZR1X, a tech powerhouse rated at 12 mpg city/19 mpg highway/14 mpg combined. Of course, since these hybrid 'Vettes feature 721 and 1,250 horsepower, respectively, their owners are unlikely to care.
Chevy hasn't been all that invested in hybrids in the past, either. In fact, with the brand only ever selling six nameplates with hybrid power in the U.S., we've got room to touch on them all today — presented from least to most fuel-efficient. We based our rankings on the highest individual EPA grade, whether it's city, highway, or combined, for the Chevrolet Silverado, Chevrolet Tahoe, Chevrolet Corvette, Chevrolet Impala, Chevrolet Malibu, and Chevrolet Bolt. In cases where vehicles have had two different hybrid systems, we picked the one with the highest fuel-economy ratings.
2009-2013 Chevrolet Silverado: 22 mpg highway
It's history time! General Motors first got into the hybrid game with the 2004 Chevrolet Silverado, but the truck was what we'd now call a mild hybrid. This means very little of the Silverado's 42-volt battery system went to actually driving the vehicle. The setup was primarily for running accessories with the engine off during certain situations — and for powering the truck's four 110-volt outlets for tools and whatnot. In the end, the rear-wheel-drive models with the 5.3-liter V8 scored 17 mpg combined with the hybrid system and 16 mpg without, while the results for the 4X4 model compared at a 16 mpg versus 15 mpg combined. Notably, the hybrid system improved the 4WD Silverado's EPA scores by 15% in the city.
Chevy dropped the Silverado hybrid after the 2007 model year, eventually reviving the truck for 2009 through 2013 with a new, two-mode hybrid system originally developed in concert with BMW and Chrysler. Without getting too deep into the details, the setup integrated two electric motors with the transmission to allow two separate assistance profiles depending on how fast the truck was going. The system could be relatively effective, too. Now relying on a 6.0-liter mill, the two-mode Silverado came in at 21 mpg in the city, 22 on the highway, and 21 combined in RWD and 20 mpg in all categories in 4WD. That's a 40% improvement over the city numbers in the most efficient gas-only truck — which carries the 5.3-liter V8.
2008-2013 Chevrolet Tahoe: 22 mpg highway
Unsurprisingly, many of the numbers for the Silverado two-mode hybrid transfer over to its Chevrolet Tahoe platform-mate. The 2008-2013 Tahoe hybrid has the same two-mode technology, the same engine, and the same EPA ratings as the 2009 Silverado. And yes, as you can tell by those dates, the Tahoe was actually first to the market.
Chevrolet's full-size body-on-frame SUVs did diverge from the brand's hybrid strategy in other ways. For instance, Chevy never tried out its mild-hybrid setup on the Tahoe or its extended-length variant, the Suburban. The Suburban wasn't configured with the two-mode setup either. GM did, however, follow its usual template with its Professional Grade division. The GMC Sierra had mild and two-mode hybrid systems in parallel with the Silverado, and the Yukon matched the Tahoe with a two-mode hybrid. The Yukon XL, like the Suburban, missed out on any hybrid help during this time.
2024-2026 Chevrolet Corvette E-Ray: 25 mpg highway
While those 2026 ZR1X models we mentioned at the start are fresh additions to Chevy's lineup, it's already possible to find them on the used-car market. For example, a low-mileage example, boasting the Carbon Fiber Pack and ZTK Performance Track Pack, went for $365,000 on Bring a Trailer in March of 2026. However, you'll have a lot more luck finding a used 2024-2026 Chevrolet Corvette E-Ray. The first editions of the very first electrified Corvette are now three model years old. Moreover, these show a fair amount of depreciation, making them that much more appealing.
From an original price of about $106,595 for the coupe — and $113,595 for the drop-top — the cars have depreciated to an average fair purchase price of $83,500and $88,700, respectively, according to Kelley Blue Book. For that sum, you can get a machine that both scores 16 mpg city, 25 mpg highway, and 19 combined with EPA and was the quickest production Corvette ever when it launched in 2024. Backed by a claimed 655 horsepower and a reputation for being way more powerful than advertised, the E-Ray races to 60 mph in 2.5 seconds. As an FYI, the quickest current 'Vette, the ZR1X, has lowered that 0-60 benchmark to 1.8 seconds, according to Car and Driver's testing
2014 Chevrolet Impala: 35 mpg highway
A one-year wonder, the 2014 Chevrolet Impala also welcomed GM's mild-hybrid tech, which provided a noticeable boost to the Impala's fuel economy. The sedan went from 21 mpg city/31 mpg highway/24 mpg combined to 24/35/28 with the EPA. For a little context, the 2014 Toyota Avalon hybrid posted EPA ratings of 40/39/40, and the most efficient Ford Taurus of 2014, with a turbocharged four-cylinder engine, achieved 22/32/26.
Used-car shoppers should further keep in mind another important advantage for the Impala. While readers have begun asking automakers to build more sedans, the Impala is already more sedan than most mass-market passenger cars on the road today. After all, this is a full-size model that represents a significant step up in cabin size from the Malibu, giving you and your passengers more room to spread out. The Impala serves up a lengthy 45.8 inches of front legroom complemented by 39.8 inches in the rear. To top it all off, if we set the Jalopnik Wayback Machine to April 25, 2013, it looks like we thought the 2014 Impala was actually a pretty damn good car when new, too.
2016-2020 Chevrolet Malibu: 47 mpg city
True, the Chevrolet Malibu died in 2024, but not before selling a pair of hybrid versions, in two distinct production runs. The first lasted from 2008 to 2010. These were sort of like the Corvettes, in that the hybrid system didn't do much for the Malibu's fuel-economy ratings. According to the EPA, the 2008 hybrid earned grades of 24 mpg city/32 mpg highway/27 mpg combined. The most efficient non-hybrid Malibu of 2008 has nearly the same EPA rating at 22/32/25. Both of these fall short of the 2010 Ford Fusion Hybrid, which had its fuel economy listed at 41/36/39.
The Malibu Hybrid sat out from 2011 to 2015, although Chevy did sell the Malibu Eco, with a mild-hybrid system, primarily in 2013. It was enough to boost the car's EPA score to 25/36/29, but its ratings ended up being the same as the standard 2014 Malibu's. The full hybrid returned to the lineup for the years 2016 to 2020, during the nameplate's ninth generation, with EPA grades of 47/46/46, besting both the Fusion Hybrid (43/39/41) and Toyota Camry Hybrid (42/38/40) when it debuted.
2016-2019 Chevrolet Volt: 42 mpg combined (gas-hybrid mode)/106 MPGe combined (EV mode)
The Chevrolet Volt plug-in hybrid was far ahead of its time when it first went on sale at the tail end of 2010. In fact, it beat the 2012 Toyota Prius plug-in to the U.S. market by more than a year. The Volt's key magic trick was that, at lower speeds, its 1.4-liter inline-4 gas engine didn't power the wheels — it only acted as a generator for the Volt's electric motor. The outcome was that the Volt had a far longer all-electric range than the Prius, since it could go for an EPA-certified 35 miles on a full charge, while the Prius was limited to 11 miles at the time. That said, the Toyota was more efficient, both in EV mode and when using gasoline. It saw an EPA score of 95 MPGe combined versus the Volt's 93 MPGe. Relying on gasoline, the Prius was good for a rating of 50 mpg combined that topped the Volt's 37 mpg by 26%.
Those grades were just for the first-gen Volt, though. Chevy redesigned the car for a second run, between 2016 and 2019 model years. These second-gen Volts raised the efficiency bar even further with an enhanced powertrain that provided up to 53 miles of all-electric driving at 106 MPGe combined, or 42 mpg.
results.summary:
Chevrolet has produced six distinct hybrid nameplates throughout its history, ranging from early mild-hybrid trucks to the high-performance electrified Corvette models currently available on the used market.

### Key Points
- The 2016-2019 Chevrolet Volt leads the brand's hybrid history with an EPA-rated 106 MPGe in EV mode and 42 mpg combined in gas-hybrid mode.
- The 2016-2020 Chevrolet Malibu Hybrid achieved 47 mpg city, outperforming contemporary competitors like the Ford Fusion and Toyota Camry hybrids.
- The 2014 Chevrolet Impala utilized mild-hybrid technology to reach 35 mpg highway, offering a full-size sedan option with significant interior legroom.
- The 2009-2013 Chevrolet Silverado and 2008-2013 Chevrolet Tahoe utilized a two-mode hybrid system to reach 22 mpg highway.
- The 2024-2026 Chevrolet Corvette E-Ray provides 655 horsepower and 25 mpg highway, representing the brand's modern shift toward performance-focused electrification.

### Why it Matters
Understanding the evolution of Chevrolet's hybrid technology helps used-car buyers identify which models offer the best balance of fuel efficiency and utility. While the brand currently focuses on high-performance hybrid Corvettes, these legacy models provide diverse options for consumers seeking electrified transportation at various price points.

results.title: Danish university DTU breach exposes data of up to 200,000 people
results.author: Ionut Ilascu
results.content:
The Technical University of Denmark (DTU) says information belonging to up to 200,000 users may have been exposed after hackers accessed its identity and access management system and downloaded a large amount of data.
The university says the attacker used compromised credentials to log into DTUBasen, its identity and access management (IAM) system, allowing access to more than two decades of user data.
In a disclosure on Friday, DTU confirmed that it cannot “determine precisely what information was downloaded or how many people have been affected.”
However, the Danish university notes that DTUBasen stores information for nearly 40,000 active users and around 160,000 former users.
Next of kin data also exposed
Potentially exposed information for current users includes Danish civil registration numbers (CPR), full names, home addresses, and profile pictures, as well as work email addresses, job titles, office locations, and other employment-related details.
The dataset also contained the names, relationships, and telephone numbers of users’ next of kin, when provided by active users.
DTU notes that in the case of former users, details about home addresses, profile pictures, and information about next of kin are automatically deleted after six months.
“This is a serious attack on DTU, and we deeply regret the uncertainty it is causing for the people whose information may have been affected,” says University Director Bjarke Bak Christensen.
“Our first priority has been to establish the extent of the attack, limit its consequences, and ensure that those affected are notified and know what steps to take,” the director added.
DTU warns that cybercriminals could use the exposed CPR numbers and other personal data for identity fraud and to make phishing attacks more convincing.
Not all notified directly
Potentially impacted individuals will be notified through e-Boks, the official mailbox system that DTU uses for sharing documents and notices with students and staff.
However, the university says it will notify all current and former employees, but not all current and former students whose CPR numbers are held by DTU.
“DTU only holds CPR numbers for a small number of guests and external partners and does not hold CPR numbers for next of kin whose contact details have been registered in DTUBasen,” the organization says.
The public dicslosure is part of DTU’s effort to reach potentially affected individuals it cannot contact directly, and the university is urging people to share it with former employees, students, guests, and external partners.
The organization says that anyone who has been an employee, student, guest, or external partner of DTU since 2003 may be affected by the data breach.
They are advised to be cautious of emails, text messages, and phone calls from individuals who appear to know about their connection with DTU or have access to personal information about them.
Passwords and sensitive information should not be disclosed in replies to unexpected communications, and sudden authentication requests or logins should be treated as suspicious.
Additionally, it is recommended to change the passwords for any other services that use the same credentials as the DTU account and place a credit alert on the affected CPR number.
Join Mikko Hyppönen and security leaders from the NFL, CHANEL, and Atlassian for a two-hour digital summit on what AI-speed attacks change, what defenders should stop doing, and how to validate, decide, fix, and re-validate at machine speed.
Save your seat
results.summary:
The Technical University of Denmark has disclosed a significant data breach involving its identity management system, potentially exposing the personal information of approximately 200,000 current and former users.

### Key Points
- Hackers accessed the DTUBasen identity and access management system using compromised credentials to download data spanning over two decades.
- Exposed information includes Danish civil registration numbers (CPR), home addresses, job titles, and contact details for next of kin.
- The breach potentially impacts anyone who has been an employee, student, guest, or external partner of the university since 2003.
- DTU is notifying affected individuals via the e-Boks system but cannot confirm the exact scope of the stolen data.
- The university advises users to monitor for identity fraud, place credit alerts on their CPR numbers, and remain vigilant against targeted phishing attempts.

### Why it Matters
This incident highlights the severe risks associated with centralized identity management systems that store long-term historical data. The exposure of sensitive government-issued identification numbers creates a long-term threat of identity theft and sophisticated social engineering attacks for the affected individuals.

results.title: As Trump's approval rating drops, Republicans begin to lose confidence in midterms
results.author: Sarah Ferris, David Wright, CNN
results.content:
Four weeks to Election Day, a growing number of House Republicans privately fear their chances of holding onto the majority are vanishing and have begun focusing on how to limit the size of a potential Democratic wave.
Inside the House GOP, Republicans have watched with alarm as President Donald Trump’s approval ratings have sunk in their own internal polling — including on traditionally red turf — over the last two weeks, according to more than a dozen people familiar with the discussions.
Now, the House GOP is entering triage mode. Republicans are discussing pulling money from once-competitive races they see as too difficult to win, including Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks in Iowa, Rep. Tom Kean in New Jersey and an open seat in Nebraska, according to three people familiar with the talks.
But the GOP does have a huge cash advantage, and not all Republicans are pessimistic. Speaker Mike Johnson is “absolutely still convinced” that he can hang onto the House and is not taking any seats “off his board,” according to a political aide. Johnson just returned from New Jersey and is planning a rally with Miller-Meeks in Iowa next week, according to his team.
The House GOP’s campaign arm, too, strenuously denies that the majority is lost.
“Thirty days out, House Republicans are on offense, and we’re outspending Democrats in the final stretch in every race,” National Republican Congressional Committee spokesperson Will Kiley said in a statement, adding, “House Republicans are going to defy history, and we’re going to win.”
The rising anxiety among Republicans, though, reflects a grim national environment that has triggered alarm bells up and down the ballot, with Senate Republicans suddenly forced on defense in red seats like Kansas — with control of both chambers of Congress up for grabs. Trump, too, is on a nationwide campaign swing, with stops in a more competitive part of Ohio, as well as deep-red territory like Texas, Oklahoma and Alabama.
“There’s a lot of close races, and it’s hard to make a prediction,” retiring GOP Rep. Dan Newhouse said this week of his party’s chances, but acknowledged, “Affordability is a big deal. People see the gas prices every single day.”
While Newhouse said his party has worked to address cost of living issues, he noted, “There’s just a lot of things making it tough right now for rural America — which I can speak to specifically — but for Americans all over the country.”
Many Republicans acknowledge to CNN that the souring national environment — fueled by soaring diesel prices, stubborn inflation and hardening opposition to the Iran war — are largely out of their control this late in the race. They say their strategy is now focused on how to limit Democrats to the slimmest majority possible — in a bid to make governing all but impossible for a potential House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries next year.
Johnson’s historically narrow majority — the slimmest since before World War II — has been a major headache for GOP leaders, with the Louisiana Republican unable to wield control of the floor on numerous occasions. Republicans want Jeffries to face the same problem.
Several people said their goal is to keep Jeffries’ margin to fewer than 10 seats. If that happens, one GOP strategist summarized: “What the f**k are you going to get done over there?”
Few Republicans believe it will be a total wipeout for their party in which Democrats win more than 30 seats. And some believe there is still a path to keeping their narrow majority, especially if gas prices drop significantly in the next four weeks. Party leaders are particularly confident about two incumbents in purple seats: Reps. Brian Fitzpatrick in Pennsylvania and Mike Lawler in New York, both in districts Kamala Harris won in 2024.
But there is growing anxiety from GOP members and aides about protecting parts of the country that haven’t elected Democrats to the House in decades — seats Trump won by double digits that are suddenly in play with incumbents who rarely face competitive general elections.
As of early October, Republicans are still planning to use a massive cash advantage to support their strongest incumbents, while turning up the heat on their top offensive targets, like Rep. Marcy Kaptur in Ohio’s 9th District, Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez in Washington’s 3rd — and drowning Democrats in spending.
The GOP’s huge cavalry of super PACs, meanwhile, helps build a firewall around their reddest turf to avert disaster, with Trump-linked groups spending in seats once considered a reach for Democrats, but are now in play, like Colorado’s 5th District, Kentucky’s 6th District and Montana’s 1st District.
“The environment is bad but Democrats still have to win on GOP terrain,” one GOP operative said.
How Republicans could still keep the House
If House Republicans are going to pull off an upset in November, they say it would come down to the party’s massive cash advantage and its aggressive gerrymandering push.
Republicans are outspending Democrats in all of the 10 most expensive House races on advertising from now until Election Day, according to data from AdImpact. That includes multimillion-dollar advantages in Democratic-held seats like Rep. Don Davis in North Carolina’s 1st District and an open seat in Maine’s 2nd District.
Much of the GOP’s spending is concentrated in newly redrawn seats in Texas and Florida, the fates of which are still highly uncertain, especially for incumbents like GOP Rep. Monica De La Cruz in Texas. But if even a handful of those seats swing toward Republicans, it could make up for losses elsewhere.
“At the end of the day, redistricting could be the lifesaver either way — either minimizing the losses or the reason we potentially hold onto the majority,” one GOP leadership aide told CNN.
Then there are the handful of swing seats where Republicans feel more upbeat because of Democratic clashes during the primaries, which left their nominees more vulnerable. That includes California’s 22nd District, Michigan’s 7th District and that open seat in Maine — where progressives beat out establishment-preferred centrists.
GOP’s messaging in final weeks
Even in a challenging midterm environment, Republicans are turning to issues that they feel give them an advantage with voters — with taxes, immigration and law enforcement figuring prominently in their campaign ads.
Tax cuts on tips, overtime and Social Security delivered by the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” were the fulfillment of a key 2024 campaign promise, and that’s been a point of emphasis. Republicans have also hammered Democrats for opposing the legislation.
“Zach Nunn voted for the largest middle class tax cut ever,” says an ad from the GOP incumbent in Iowa’s competitive 3rd District.
An analysis of AdImpact data found that about one-third of GOP ads in House races in September focused on tax policy, making it the top issue tracked by the firm.
Immigration, which ranked fourth, has been another key argument for Republicans. “Stelson wants you to pay for criminal illegal immigrants’ healthcare,” says an ad from the House GOP’s main super PAC, Congressional Leadership Fund, targeting the Democrat in Pennsylvania’s 10th District.
GOP advertisers also produced dozens of ads touting their support for law enforcement and accusing Democrats of being soft on crime. Several begin with grisly accounts of local crimes, juxtaposed with rhetoric from Democrats calling for criminal justice reform. “Attention all criminals, do we have some good news for you: Christina Hines, the liberal Ann Arbor prosecutor, is running for Congress,” says one ad airing in the competitive race for Michigan’s 10th District.
Other specific issues have also animated these key races, including Republicans’ sustained focus on transgender policies, an issue they’ve used to attack Democrats since it proved effective in the 2024 campaign. As a result, Democrats have increasingly taken to the airwaves to rebut the criticism, such as Kaptur in Ohio’s 9th District.
Republicans say the Democrats’ quick response to the transgender politics attacks show that it’s an effective issue — and believe it’s been making a dent in internal polling.
“Here’s the truth: I voted with Republicans to keep transgender ideology out of our schools because parents know what’s best for their kids, and boys should not play in girls’ sports,” Kaptur says in one ad.
This story has been updated with additional information.
results.summary:
House Republicans are shifting to a defensive strategy as internal polling and a challenging national environment threaten their narrow majority four weeks before the November election.

### Key Points
- House GOP leadership is considering pulling funding from difficult races to focus resources on protecting vulnerable incumbents.
- Republicans maintain a significant cash advantage and are outspending Democrats in the 10 most expensive House races.
- Internal party concerns are driven by declining approval ratings for Donald Trump and persistent voter anxiety over inflation and gas prices.
- The party is emphasizing tax policy, immigration, and law enforcement in campaign advertisements to regain momentum.
- Strategists hope to limit potential Democratic gains to fewer than 10 seats to prevent a functional governing majority for a potential Speaker Hakeem Jeffries.

### Why it Matters
The outcome of these races will determine which party controls the legislative agenda and the ability of the next administration to pass key policies. A narrow majority for either side could lead to significant gridlock, mirroring the legislative difficulties experienced during the current congressional session.

results.title: Mysterious coded Napoleon letter has been cracked after 217 years
results.author: unexplained-mysteries.com
results.content:
Archaeology & History
    Mysterious coded Napoleon letter has been cracked after 217 years
    By 
T.K. Randall
October 3, 2026
    
     
    
    
        
Image: AI-generated (Midjourney)
        
    
    The letter, which was written in code, had remained a complete mystery as the accompanying key had been lost.
			
     More than two centuries after it was originally written, the contents of a mysterious coded letter have finally been revealed thanks to the capabilities of one of the latest artificial intelligence models.
Penned by Napoleon Bonaparte, the letter had been sent to French general Auguste de Marmont in 1809 by the Viceroy of Italy (who happened to be Napoleon's stepson).
It begins in clear French, but then the rest of the letter is written in a strange code consisting of numbers, letters and inverted symbols.
Originally, a key would have been used to decipher it, but this had been lost long ago, meaning that nobody had ever been able to actually decode the message and find out what it says.
Now, though, cybersecurity engineer  Carter Church has finally found a way to decipher the mysterious letter using artificial intelligence.The deciphering process, which used GPT-6 Astra, took a mere 6 hours.
The decoded letter had given General Marmont a strategic overview of the positions and strength of French and allied armies, along with information about Austrian forces.
It also urged Marmont to prepare to march without being intimidated by relatively small enemy forces, saying that Austria was about to be attacked from all sides and was "hastening towards her ruin."
"I used GPT-6 Astra to break an unsolved cipher to one of Napoleon's generals that had gone unread for 217 years," Church wrote on X.
"What makes this impressive isn't actually the codebreaking, but that Astra completed the entire multi-modal workflow in six hours from a single image and goal."
    
    Source: 
Mail Online

### Key Points
- The letter, written in 1809, contained a complex cipher of numbers, letters, and inverted symbols that had remained unreadable for over two centuries.

- The message provided General Marmont with a strategic overview of French and allied troop positions while detailing the vulnerability of Austrian forces.

results.title: How ‘Unmasking a Monster: Aileen Wuornos’ Used AI to Bring a Serial Killer Back to Life
results.author: Elisabeth Garber-Paul
results.content:
At first, Unmasking a Monster: Aileen Wuornos, ID’s new true-crime documentary, seems like a familiar look into America’s most famous female serial killer. As the first episode starts, there’s an archival voiceover from Wuornos, who was executed in 2001, professing that she has to tell the truth about the seven murders she was accused of committing; there’s a homicide detective who was on the case, recounting how he came in contact with the murderer; there’s a friend of Wuornos’ talking about the disbelief she felt when she found out about her crimes. Over the audio clips, images cut between trial footage, modern-day interviews, and staged reenactments.
But those reenactments aren’t being done by actors. Instead, as noted in an early title card disclosing the use of “advanced generative VFX,” they feature AI-enhanced digitizations of recreated scenes from Wuornos’ life. When the series depicts Wuornos pointing a gun into the camera to show what a victim would have seen in his last moments, this is the real Aileen Wuornos. Almost.
Unmasking a Monster, which premiered on ID and is now streaming on HBO Max, is the first documentary to use this kind of AI-aided visual effects technology — what Stephen Dost, vice president of Arrow Media, the company that developed the process, calls a “digital mask” — to put a more realistic layer over re-created scenes performed by actors. True-crime media has changed over the last decade, explains Jason Sarlanis, president of Investigation Discovery, which helped produce the series. No longer are viewers content with expert interviews and staged reenactments covering the arc of a story in 44 minutes. “What has changed for us, in terms of how we research and develop these stories, has come down to access to materials and access to people close to the case,” he says. “Hearing their unvarnished perspective and then supplementing that with as many real archival materials as possible.”
But what AI offered was a way for them to give the viewer the sensation of seeing archival material when none existed. According to Sarlanis, ID’s viewers have consistently complained that they’re turned off by reenactments. “They’re just not interested,” he says. “They want something as visually authentic as possible. What these digital prosthetics have allowed us to do is transport the viewer there in the most seamless, authentic way that we could do in reenactments that we weren’t able to do before.”
The idea for the series, explains Sarlanis, came over drinks about three years ago. He was talking with Dost, whose Arrow Media is a frequent producer of ID’s true-crime series, about a show he’d recently seen, the U.K. comedy Deep Fake Neighbor Wars, which used rudimentary AI technology to superimpose celebrity faces over impersonators acting out scenes. The tech didn’t quite land, but they could tell that in a few years, it could be nearly seamless. “That lit a light bulb up for us,” Sarlanis says. “We could take similar technology, executed in a far more thoughtful and nuanced way, and lend it to re-creations — which are such a big part of the history of documentary — and unlock a whole new method of telling stories.”
Dost agreed the technology was worth exploring, and started thinking about whose story he would want to use it to tell. “Because you have to have a good reason why,” he says. “The tech for the sake of the tech is not interesting.” A true-crime vet — he’d gotten his start in the mid-1990s as an intern at Court TV — he kept coming back to Wuornos. “Everything she had been through — from her mother abandoning her as a child, to being assaulted at the age of 14, [to] giving up a child — all these horrible things that happened to her, you could see it on her face,” he says. “Her face told a story.”
Dost and Sarlanis are aware of the stigma AI might bring to the project. Part of why it took three years, they say, is because they wanted to think through the implications of including this type of technology in their show. “This was a human production,” Dost says. “We had 70-plus people. We had the best writers, interviewers. Despite the visual-effects twist, it’s a very traditional documentary. I think knowing what AI can do — and more importantly, what it can’t do — is the way to use it right.”
One guideline they gave themselves was that those whose digital likeness would be used in the re-creations — other than Wuornos, a public figure — had to give their consent. “If we’re going to use the technology on them as a character, [we needed] full, written permission,” Dost says. “We did not use it whenever there was a question mark.” One such question mark was Mike Joyner, an undercover investigator who’d worked on the case, who they’d interviewed several years earlier for a different project, but had since died. “When we filmed that interview, it was before we even thought of using this tech,” says Dost. In 1991, Joyner had posed as a criminal and chatted up Wuornos at the Last Resort bar, a biker hangout in Florida where the serial killer was ultimately apprehended, and their lengthy conversation was something the producers knew they wanted to include. But instead of transposing Joyner’s real face over an actor, they opted to just go with an actor who looked like him, since he wasn’t alive to consent.
“Originally, we only intended to do this process with Aileen, and then we realized it would be interesting to see the other characters, [so] we went back to them because they would need to sign an amended release,” explains Dost. “But everyone very readily agreed to it.”
Additionally, Dost says, they didn’t use AI in writing any part of the show. The scripts were written based on their own reporting, including court documents, investigation transcripts, and interviews with detectives, witnesses, and even Laurie Valdez, an old friend of Wuornos’ who’d never previously spoken with the press. “Nothing is made up,” Dost says. “Everything here is based on a transcript, based on something that our [interviewee] told us that they remembered happening. So it’s as authentic as you can possibly be.”
Morag Peacock, the Scottish actress who is the basis for the Wuornos reenactments, studied hours of tape to try to mimic the serial killer’s emotions — “her quirks, her mannerisms, how she used her eyes quite expressively,” she explains. Yet even after the VFX was laid over her performance, she could see herself shine through. “I could recognize myself in it. “I said, ‘I feel like it’s my eyes.’ And Stephen said, ‘It is. We’ve done nothing to change them,’” she says. “It isn’t a completely fabricated image. It’s me with a mask on top.” (One thing that’s less recognizable is Peacock’s voice; though she spoke in an American accent for the filming, Sarlanis notes that they did “train a model on real archival audio of Aileen’s voice that was then utilized to tweak her vocal performance — but the underlying performance is all Morag.”)
Peacock says she had been hesitant to take the job because of its use of the new technology. “AI can be very triggering, isn’t it?” she says. “It’s something that can be used well, or like any tool, can be abused.” But overall, she was pleased with the scenes that she saw, though she hadn’t watched the whole series when we spoke.
Sarlanis, for one, isn’t worried that the use of AI will overshadow the story the series is trying to tell. “If anything, it might be a beacon to bring attention to the new reporting and the incredible access,” he says. “In a world where true crime is one of the most in-demand genres, there are so many options for viewers. If you do not have an element that can bring attention to your project, it can fall on deaf ears.”
But like Peacock, who saw the technology “as a costume that’s added at the end,” Dost and Sarlanis insist the AI adds are simply high-tech makeup and prosthetics. “AI cannot act,” says Dost. “It can look at Morag and detect even tiny micro-expressions in the way that she’s delivering a line, so that when the digital mask is applied, it’s copying every little emotion.”
There’s a reason they didn’t want to simply add prompts to an AI bot and have it spit out a fully reenacted scene. “It has to start with something human,” says Dost. It’s not really different, he says, from the elaborate transformation Charlize Theron went through for the 2003 Wuornos biopic Monster. “Why did she want to look like the real Aileen? Part of it was exactly the same reason: Her face told a story,” he says. “And what we’re doing is the 2026 version of that.”
results.summary:
The new Investigation Discovery documentary series Unmasking a Monster utilizes advanced generative AI to create digital masks over actors, aiming to provide a more authentic visual experience for viewers.

### Key Points
- The series, now streaming on HBO Max, is the first documentary to use AI-aided visual effects to recreate scenes from the life of serial killer Aileen Wuornos.
- Arrow Media developed the "digital mask" technology, which overlays AI-enhanced imagery onto human performances to simulate archival footage.
- Producers required written consent from all living individuals whose likenesses were digitally recreated for the series.
- The production team emphasized that all scripts were written by humans based on court documents, transcripts, and original interviews.
- Actress Morag Peacock provided the physical performance for the Wuornos reenactments, with her own eyes and micro-expressions preserved under the digital layer.

### Why it Matters
This production signals a significant shift in documentary filmmaking by using generative AI to replace traditional, often criticized, reenactment methods. By framing the technology as a modern evolution of prosthetic makeup, the creators are testing audience acceptance of synthetic media in factual storytelling.

results.title: Private capital is reshaping Hollywood moviemaking
results.author: Laya Neelakandan
results.content:
At the Toronto International Film Festival last month, audiences saw "Wicked" star Cynthia Erivo return to the big screen for her newest movie, "Prima Facie."
Behind the scenes, there was a notable difference.
While "Wicked" was a massive Universal undertaking, Erivo's new movie was produced in part by Camelback Productions, a smaller Hollywood venture aiming to fund independent film, according to CEO Anita Verma-Lallian.
She's one of many private investors who are betting big on Hollywood as the moviegoing landscape shifts and a handful of indie films catch fire.
"It's a different point of view to invest in these projects," Verma-Lallian said. "It's been so hard for people that are not in Hollywood to get into the industry ... We've been able to fund stories that otherwise would have had a hard time getting greenlit by the traditional studio system."
Camelback has also produced films "Doin' It" and "Runner," with stars such as Lilly Singh and Owen Wilson.
Big blockbuster films such as this year's "The Odyssey" and "The Devil Wears Prada 2" are still the domain of legacy Hollywood studios. But with the number of annual releases dwindling, and with forthcoming consolidation among major players Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery, there's growing opportunity for smaller production companies to hit it big.
And while the business of making movies is still generally capital-intensive, recent breakouts including "Backrooms" and "Obsession" have found success on lower budgets.
To thread the needle, private capital is buying into production companies, acquiring the infrastructure and diving deeper into the financing structure of entertainment. For example, private equity firm Silver Lake backs talent agency WME, and Blackstone is behind content studio Candle Media.
According to consulting firm AlixPartners' 2026 Media and Entertainment Industry Predictions report, private equity investors in media are growing with precision, especially as studios and audience aggregators increasingly become vertically integrated.
While the cost of entry has increased, private investors are eager to own intellectual property and audiences, the report said.
"Private equity can build scaled, defensible businesses that profit regardless of which large media player owns the next blockbuster, effectively ensuring a central role in the future media value chain," the report read.
And while deep-pocketed companies such as Netflix and Amazon continue to raise the bar for content spend to make or acquire new media, traditional studios are finding new ways to keep pace.
For Verma-Lallian, investing in independent film means that she can complete movies on a much faster timeline than traditional studios can.
"A lot of times, if you go through the traditional Hollywood system, it could literally take five to 10 years from the time of inception," she said. "Whereas if you're doing it independently, we've made some movies in as quickly as a year."
This can often mean lower production costs and a quicker return on investment.
Verma-Lallian, whose background is in real estate investing, said Hollywood has proven to be a largely attractive market for herself and other nontypical private investors looking to diversify their portfolios.
She said they're also jumping on the opportunity at a time when existing financing models are weakening.
"I think the traditional sources [of financing] are starting to decline, and they're becoming a lot more risk-averse," she said. "I do also believe now with more independent films being funded and going to different pools of capital, you're able to do more."
While Verma-Lallian said she doesn't believe private capital will become the primary source of financing in Hollywood, she said the agility of investors can potentially put pressure on the incumbents.
"Hollywood is incredibly traditional, and it's very old-fashioned in the way it operates, which always I find so ironic, because ... Hollywood's so progressive, but the way that the studio systems work, it's just a very dated process from my experience," she said.
Still, studios and private investors are racing to get new storylines to the big screen. For investors, that means capitalizing on the intellectual property that hasn't already been used, according to Alex Michael, senior managing director at investment firm LionTree.
"What is clear to me is that IP has never been more valuable. It's never been harder to find," Michael said at the Financial Times' Business of Entertainment Summit last month. "But if you have great IP, you can monetize it in ways that no one could have imagined 10 years ago."
LionTree is an independent banking firm, investing in companies such as Fanatics and Fubo and advising high-profile deals such as Amazon's acquisition of MGM and the merger of CBS and Viacom. It's also investing in Paramount, pending the close of its deal with Warner Bros. Discovery.
Michael added that the entertainment industry as a whole is becoming more diversified, with retail entrants such as Gap and Mattel's Barbie, which are also helping to support the economics of the sector.
With the entry of private capital, Hollywood faces not only an economic shift but also a cultural shift in the types of movies being made.
Private investors often tell more diverse stories, take more risks and try to reach an audience that is hungry for content, said Lata Krishnan, a tech investor entering the Hollywood market.
"The big studios are often legacy organizations focused on a certain type set of films, and I think private capital has the ability now ... to invest in films that are not traditional and that give voices to stories in a different way," she told CNBC.
The result, she said, is that audiences get exposed to stories they haven't seen before.
That also means the next wave of movies must keep up with the new generation of moviegoers, who are increasingly drawn to diverse content they can relate to. Part of that shift is the rise of short-form and creator content, which can find its way onto the big screen — as in the case of YouTuber Curry Barker's "Obsession" — in a bid to draw Generation Z to the box office.
This dynamic also puts new people in the driver's seat.
"It's my capital. I don't have to check in with anyone," Krishnan said. "So we explore a theme, a story, the actors and the production team, and we can make quick decisions."
Private investors have the flexibility and speed to jump on trends fast and fill a gap first, according to Elan Gale, a Hollywood producer and investor. He's the co-founder of QWGmire, an independent film financing company.
Gale, who has also worked on the production of shows such as "The Bachelor," said audiences are "hungry" to get back into the theater for something new and original.
"I think the primary upside for filmmakers is that private equity investors are less likely to get into the nitty-gritty of the creative process and allow some of the exploration and some of the freedom that studios maybe can't give filmmakers because they're significantly larger companies with significantly more restrictive development processes," Gale said.
"I think Hollywood is reshaping around private capital, around brands and around content creators in ways that are really meaningful," he said. "A lot of the successes that people have seen recently are a little too hard to ignore."
results.summary:
Private investors and independent production companies are increasingly financing Hollywood films, challenging the traditional studio system by offering faster production timelines and more diverse storytelling opportunities for audiences.

### Key Points
- Independent firms like Camelback Productions are bypassing traditional studio greenlight processes to fund films featuring stars like Cynthia Erivo and Owen Wilson.
- Private equity firms, including Silver Lake and Blackstone, are acquiring infrastructure and intellectual property to secure central roles in the evolving media value chain.
- Independent financing models can reduce production timelines from five to ten years down to as little as one year.
- Investors are targeting niche and diverse content to attract younger demographics, including Generation Z, who are increasingly drawn to creator-led projects.
- Consulting firm AlixPartners reports that private equity is building scaled, defensible businesses that remain profitable regardless of which major media player dominates the box office.

### Why it Matters
The influx of private capital is forcing a structural shift in Hollywood by introducing agility and risk-taking that legacy studios often lack. This trend allows for a more diverse range of stories to reach theaters while providing investors with new opportunities to monetize valuable intellectual property.

results.title: US-Russia Peace Talks Now Include Multi-Billion Dollar Oil Deal Tied to Trump Negotiators: NYT
results.author: Kathryn Wilkens
results.content:
US-Russia Peace Talks Now Include Multi-Billion Dollar Oil Deal Tied to Trump Negotiators: NYT
President Donald Trump’s negotiations with Russia over ending the war in Ukraine have reportedly become intertwined with a massive oil deal involving business figures connected to his two leading envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
The New York Times reported Saturday that a group seeking to purchase the international assets of Russian energy giant Lukoil includes billionaire investor Todd Boehly, who has donated $2 million to MAGA-related causes, as well as Middle Eastern investors with business connections to Kushner and Witkoff’s family. The U.S. International Development Finance Corporation would also participate in the deal.
The proposed transaction, which still requires approval from both Washington and Moscow, covers Lukoil holdings around the globe, including oil fields, refineries, and gas stations.
Russian President Vladimir Putin personally raised the idea during a Sept. 5 Kremlin meeting with Witkoff and Kushner, according to the Times. Putin pitched the sale as a way to demonstrate that Russia could resume doing business with the United States, and the two Trump envoys agreed to work on it, believing a deal could improve relations with Moscow and help reduce energy prices.
“But the deal is also a lucrative one for the buyers: U.S. approval for the sale would release the assets from American sanctions, instantly increasing their value,” wrote the Times.
Witkoff struck a notably warm tone during that Sept. 5 meeting, thanking the Russian leader for hosting him and saying the memories of their meetings would be “right at the top” of the stories he would tell after retiring.

Back to the comments/content issues. Reader Expat2Uruguay noted that the comments quality had declined, to the degree that she did not find them to be terribly informative. We certainly are not at the extremely high and insightful as we had early in the Iran war. Some of that is likely due to fatigue with an attritional war as well as some dropping out for a while due to personal demands such as travel (but we do seem to have lost raspberry jam; her e-mail address, with a personal domain name, is no longer working).
Covering the Iran war, which many of you have said you have appreciated keenly, has become more difficult as the US fog-making has increased and the Iran side has gone from being highly reliable to less so. On top of that, Trump’s success in manipulating paper oil markets has wrong-footed some top energy analysts who pay attention to fundamentals (and their upset about that skews the commentary from some of them….who also opine on macroeconomics, which is not their beat and it shows). Trump’s ongoing gaslighting and shows of extreme aggression are now well in the Groundhog Day terrain, which is designed to and has had some success in drowning out analysis and commentary.
On top of that, many commentators who have favored the Iran side (if nothing else by virtue of being anti-genocide, ani-imperialism, and/or anti-Trump) have become frustrated with some inexplicable-seeming Iran responses, like not attacking US naval vessels when it seems to be able to do so, or letting more oil transit, and have taken to trying to force-fit evidence into their priors, or worse, ad-hominem attacks on sources that don’t hew to their views. On the transit issue specifically, Trita Parsi had a good talk with Mario Nawfal in which that topic came up. Parsi, who recall has very good contacts on the Iran side and with the negotiators, said more oil was being allowed to pass. He would have treated that as contested or exaggerated if anyone on the Iran side were disputing that in a serious way. Parsi did point out that the US was over-hyping the amount getting out by citing figures on peak days, when passage on other days was much lower. He added this operation is taking place at great cost to the US, implying it can’t be sustained for all that long.
And we have not been all that excited about the argument over how much oil is actually transiting. Even if you take the numbers from private sector sources deemed to be shills, it’s still markedly below pre-war levels. The world will have to engage in a combination of drawing down more on badly shrunken inventories and using less (which means recessions). This is still an energy starvation diet. If you need 2000 calories a day to survive, you will starve if limited to 500 or 1000 calories a day. It just happens more slowly on 1000 calories a day.
But wars are not won with narratives. They are won with logistics, armaments, force discipline and size, and in the case of Iran, a geography which makes it extremely conquest-resistant. Narratives can, however, serve to keep a losing or disadvantaged combatant in the game beyond what ought to be his quit date, resulting in higher cost to both him and his opponent.
There is more and more evidence of US depletion becoming even more extreme despite the Administration bluster. Brandon Weichert discussed with Karen Kwaitkowski and others that the US moving in another aircraft carrier and more ground forces may be a rotation and not a bulking up. Trump has notably failed to deliver on a key threat of tanker-for-tanker destruction.
On the energy side, one reason for Iran being more measured than it logically should be may be the result of actions on other energy fronts. Putin had just announced there will be no more diesel exports until sanctions are lifted. China has halted energy exports when its refiners have been described as the only meaningful remaining global spare capacity. US refiners have scheduled, as in contracted-for maintenance coming, so US output looks destined to drop off even if there are no mishaps like a Gulf hurricane or a big outage. The successful US pressure to get the EU to tap into its diesel reserves is yet another band-aid over a gunshot wound.
Finally, one reader argued we should not be covering Iran but finance. However, this is neither the runup to the crisis, where there was a lot of data about certain parts of the equation, like reset terms on subprime mortgages, and and active and expert econoblogsphere ferreting out more, nor is this a Cyprus banking or Greek bailout crisis, where a lot could be divined from negotiation dynamics, regulatory matters, and fundamentals. The action now is in private debt and even journalists who have put shoulder to wheel (as in have done a lot of interviews) have admitted they have not gotten very far. One indictor: look at the absolutely enormous it has taken for Ed Zitron to reach some conclusions about the economics of the big AI players.
And readers make clear they are not interested in anything that does not suit their anti-imperialist priors. Reader Expat2Uruguay pointed to a recent post, De-Dollarization Is a YouTube Urban Legend, which got no comments for many many hours and in the end garnered only a few. Why should I bother telling readers what is going on when no one is interested? At least when I took a very unpopular view during the Greek bailout crisis, that the plucky Greeks would not prevail (and they did not), I got extremely heated pushback. Being completely ignored says this audience has very little appetite for analysis…either on finance topics generally or on findings that do not conform to erroneous but emotionally appealing story lines.
